section: Databases and Storage Engines at Big-Tech Scale
hook: A profile, a friend list, a "last seen" timestamp. Why do records this tiny need their own kind of storage?
title: Tiny records, constant changes, millisecond reads
body:
Blocks, files and objects handle bulky data. But a global app with 1 billion users also stores millions of tiny things: the user profile, the friend list, the "last seen" timestamp, message metadata, payment records. This is **structured data**: rows, keys, documents and graph edges that the app reads and changes one small piece at a time.

Each record is small, changes often, and must come back in a few milliseconds. That trio, not raw size, shapes database design at big-tech scale.
takeaway: Size doesn't shape a database. Small, frequent and fast does.
deeper:
**Per operation, not per gigabyte:** With bulk files you pay per byte stored. With structured data you pay per operation. A tiny update that forces a big disk write, or a lookup that checks many places, gets multiplied by billions of rows and constant traffic.

**Where the cost is decided:** At the bottom sits the **storage engine**, the code that lays out row bytes on one machine's disk. It sets the price of every read and write on a node.

**Then the spread:** Above the engine sit distributed databases. Google, Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix each spread rows over thousands of machines, and each made a different bet on one question: where do you put consistency, and what do you give up to get scale?

**The usual ending:** One company rarely runs one database. Profiles, money, messages, the social graph and ML features each have a different shape, so each tends to get its own store.

quiz.q: A team stores constantly updated user profiles in the same system they use for large write-once video files. Reads feel sluggish. What is the mismatch?
quiz.a: Profiles are tiny, change often and need millisecond reads, so per-operation overhead dominates. A store tuned for big write-once blobs optimizes bytes, not small frequent operations.

mcq.q: What mainly shapes database design for structured data at big-tech scale?
options: Small records that change often and need millisecond reads
The total volume of bytes stored for each user
The need to store large write-once media files
Sequential scans over whole columnar datasets
mcq.why: Structured records are tiny, updated often and read in milliseconds, so per-operation cost dominates the design.

hook: SQL, replication and sharding barely care how one layer of your database works. That layer sets your bill.
title: The storage engine decides your hardware bill
body:
A database stacks layers: SQL, replication, sharding. Those upper layers mostly ignore how bytes land on disk. That job belongs to the **storage engine**, the part that stores and finds data on one node. It answers three questions: where does a new write go, how do I find a key again, and how do I reclaim space from old versions?

Those answers set the cost of every single read and write. Multiply by big-tech traffic, and the engine decides how many servers and SSDs you buy.
takeaway: The layer nobody looks at sets the bill everyone pays.
deeper:
**Why the split helps:** Because upper layers ignore the engine, companies can swap it. MySQL runs on InnoDB or on RocksDB. Instagram swapped Cassandra's Java engine for RocksDB. Espresso and Docstore keep InnoDB under their own distribution layers.

**Two families:** B-tree engines update data in place: InnoDB, PostgreSQL's heap plus B-tree indexes, WiredTiger's B-tree mode, DynamoDB's storage nodes. LSM-tree engines never update in place. They write new files and merge them later: RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase, ScyllaDB, Pebble in CockroachDB.

**How it reaches the bill:** A small per-operation difference, times billions of rows and constant traffic, becomes a difference in fleet size. Meta moved its main MySQL database from compressed InnoDB to MyRocks and ended up with fewer than half as many UDB servers. Same SQL, same applications, different engine.

quiz.q: Two teams run the same SQL schema on the same replication setup. One needs twice as many servers for the same traffic. Nothing above the storage layer differs. Where do you look first?
quiz.a: The storage engine. It sets the disk cost of each read, write and stored byte on every node, and those per-operation costs multiply into fleet size.

mcq.q: Which three questions does a storage engine answer?
options: Where writes go, how keys are found, how old space is reclaimed
How SQL is parsed, how plans are chosen, how joins run
Which replica leads, which follows, which takes over on failure
How keys map to shards, how shards map to zones and regions
mcq.why: The engine is the single-node layer: write placement, key lookup and space reclamation. Parsing, replication and sharding sit above it.

hook: You change one row. One engine rewrites it where it lives. The other never touches the old copy again.
title: Update in place, or never update in place
body: Every engine must decide what happens when a row changes. **B-tree** engines find the page holding the row and change it there: one current copy per key, simple reads, but writes land at random spots on disk. **LSM-tree** engines never update in place. They write the new version to new files and merge files later in the background. Writes become sequential, but one key may live in several files until the merge. That single choice drives most differences in read, write and space cost.
takeaway: B-trees pay at write time. LSM-trees pay later, in the background.
deeper:
**Update in place:** The write goes wherever the row already lives, which can be anywhere on disk. That means random I/O, and partly filled pages waste space. But there is exactly one current copy of each row, so reads stay predictable. InnoDB, PostgreSQL, WiredTiger's B-tree mode and DynamoDB's storage nodes work this way.

**Never update in place:** Updates and deletes are appended as new data. The foreground write is cheap and sequential. The bill comes later: reads may look in several files, and old versions take space until compaction removes them. RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase, ScyllaDB and Pebble work this way.

**Neither wins everywhere:** The fair comparison uses three numbers: write, read and space amplification. Read-heavy transactional work tends to favor B-trees. Write-heavy, large, cost-sensitive data on flash tends to favor LSM-trees.

quiz.q: A key is updated five times in an hour. How many versions of it might sit on disk in a B-tree engine versus an LSM engine?
quiz.a: B-tree: one, overwritten in its page. LSM: possibly several, one per newer file, until compaction merges them and drops the stale ones.

mcq.q: Which engine family writes updates to new files and merges them later?
options: LSM-tree engines, like RocksDB and Cassandra
B-tree engines, like InnoDB and WiredTiger
B-tree engines, like PostgreSQL and DynamoDB
Both families, once a page fills up
mcq.why: LSM-trees never update in place; they append new versions to new files and compact later. B-tree engines change the page where the row lives.

hook: Your app writes 1 KB. Over time, the disk quietly writes far more. Where do the extra bytes come from?
title: You wrote 1 KB. Your disk wrote 10.

stat.label: write amplification: 1 KB in, 10 KB to disk

body: A database never writes just your bytes. It logs them, rewrites whole pages around them, and later merges the files that hold them. **Write amplification** is bytes actually written to disk divided by bytes you wrote. Write 1 KB, watch 10 KB hit the disk over time, and it is 10. The extra bytes are not free. They burn SSD endurance and eat disk bandwidth that could serve users.
takeaway: Size disks for user writes times amplification, not user writes.
deeper:
**Key words, over time:** Amplification is not only what happens at write time. In a B-tree, a 100-byte row change can force a 16 KB page write, plus a WAL record, plus InnoDB's doublewrite copy. In an LSM-tree, the foreground write is small and sequential, but compaction rewrites each byte roughly once per level as data moves down.

**Same number, different shape:** Two engines can have similar totals with very different patterns. LSM writes are large, sequential and compressed, which suits flash. B-tree writes are page-sized and scattered.

**The capacity trap:** The disk bandwidth you need is user write rate times write amplification. Teams that size disks for user writes alone find background work, especially compaction, saturating the device and stalling the database.

**Why SSDs care:** Flash cells survive a limited number of program/erase cycles. Every amplified byte spends that budget, so SSD endurance belongs in the compaction decision.

quiz.q: Your service writes 50 MB/s of user data into an engine with write amplification 10. The SSD sustains 300 MB/s of writes. Will it keep up?
quiz.a: No. The disk must absorb about 500 MB/s (50 × 10), well past 300 MB/s, so background work falls behind even though user traffic looks modest.

mcq.q: An engine shows a write amplification of 10. What does that mean?
options: The disk writes 10 bytes for every byte the user writes
Each write is copied to 10 different replica nodes
A read must check 10 files to find one key
The disk holds 10 bytes for every live byte
mcq.why: Write amplification is disk bytes written divided by user bytes written. Files checked is read amplification; bytes held is space amplification.

hook: Your table holds 100 GB of live rows. The disk says far more is used. What is filling the difference?
title: Read and space amplification: looks and leftovers
body: Write cost is one of three numbers. **Read amplification** counts how many disk reads, or places to look, one query needs. An engine with one known home per row scores low; one that checks several files scores higher. **Space amplification** is bytes on disk divided by live data. Old versions, deleted rows not yet cleaned up, and half-empty pages all take disk while holding nothing you can read. With write amplification, these three numbers compare any two engines.
takeaway: "Faster" means nothing until you say which amplification paid for it.
deeper:
**B-tree profile:** Low read amplification. The tree is 3 to 5 levels deep with the top cached, so a point read costs about one disk read. Space suffers: pages split and are often left 50 to 70 percent full. Meta measured 25 to 30 percent wasted space from fragmentation across its InnoDB fleet.

**LSM profile:** Higher read amplification, because a key may sit in the memtable or any of several files, checked newest first. Bloom filters and a block cache pull it back down. Space depends on compaction. Leveled keeps it around 1.1 times the live data. Tiered lets duplicates live longer and may briefly need double the space during a big merge.

**Why the vocabulary matters:** "LSM is faster" is vague until you name what got faster and which cost paid for it. The three numbers turn an argument into something you can measure.

quiz.q: Two databases hold the same 100 GB of live rows. One uses 130 GB of disk, the other 110 GB. Name two things that could fill the extra space.
quiz.a: Half-empty pages left by B-tree splits, and stale versions or tombstoned rows that LSM compaction has not removed yet. Both occupy disk without holding live data.

mcq.q: Which of these increases space amplification?
options: Deleted rows still on disk awaiting cleanup
Bloom filters rejecting files during reads
Reads that check several SSTables per lookup
Upper tree levels cached in memory
mcq.why: Space amplification is disk bytes over live bytes. Dead rows occupy disk without adding live data; the other options affect reads.

hook: Engineers have argued B-tree versus LSM for decades. A three-letter rule explains why nobody wins.
title: Read, write, space: optimize two, pay for the third
body: Every engine pays three costs: reads, writes (updates) and space. The **RUM conjecture**, a useful rule of thumb, says you can optimize two of them but not all three at once. Cut one, and the cost moves to another. A B-tree buys fast reads with page-sized writes and wasted page space. A tiered LSM buys cheap writes with extra reads and extra space. So no engine is a universal winner. Each is a point in the trade-off, and your workload picks the point.
takeaway: Every engine is a trade. Know which two corners you're buying.
deeper:
**Walk the triangle:** A B-tree favors reads: about one disk read per point lookup and excellent range scans. It pays in write amplification and fragmented pages. A leveled LSM favors space and sequential writes, paying with heavy compaction rewrites and more read effort. A tiered LSM cuts write amplification further but raises both read and space costs.

**Knobs trace the same curve:** Inside RocksDB you choose leveled, universal (tiered) or FIFO compaction. Bloom filters spend memory to save reads. Block caches trade RAM for fewer disk hits. Each knob slides you along the trade-off. None escapes it.

**Turn it into questions:** What is the write rate per node? Are reads point lookups or range scans? Does data expire? Is space or SSD endurance the expensive resource? The answers name the two corners worth optimizing, and the cost you agree to eat.

quiz.q: A vendor claims its engine beats B-trees on reads, beats LSMs on writes, and has the smallest disk footprint of all. What do you ask?
quiz.a: Where the cost went. By the RUM conjecture you can't win all three, so look for the hidden price: memory, background work, or a narrow benchmark workload.

mcq.q: Tiered compaction lowers write amplification. Per the RUM conjecture, what usually rises in exchange?
options: Read and space amplification
Only tail write latency
Memtable memory per node
The number of B-tree levels
mcq.why: Leaving overlapping files around saves rewrites, but reads check more files and duplicates stay on disk longer.

hook: A table has billions of rows. A B-tree still finds any one of them in about one disk read. How?

predict.q: A B-tree indexes billions of rows. How many levels deep is it, typically?
options: 3 to 5
About 30
About 100

title: Billions of rows, 3 to 5 levels, about 1 disk read
body: Finding one row among billions sounds like it should take many disk reads. A **B-tree** (in practice a B+tree) avoids that by being wide and shallow. It is a tree of fixed-size pages, often 4 to 16 KB. Inner pages hold keys and child pointers; leaf pages hold rows or pointers to them. Each page holds a few hundred keys, the **fan-out**, so billions of rows need only 3 to 5 levels. The top levels stay cached in memory, so a point read costs about one disk read.
takeaway: Wide pages make short trees. Short trees make one-read lookups.
deeper:
**Fan-out does the work:** Each level multiplies reachable rows by a few hundred. Three to five levels cover billions. A binary tree would need about 30 levels for a billion keys.

**Why OLTP loves it:** Each key has exactly one home, so read latency is stable. It does not depend on how much background work is pending. Range scans are cheap too: leaf pages are sorted and linked, so a scan walks consecutive leaves.

**The catch:** The disk and buffer pool deal in whole pages. Change one row and you dirty, then eventually rewrite, a whole page. That is the source of B-tree write amplification and, with page splits, its space overhead. The same page structure that makes reads fast makes small writes expensive.

quiz.q: Memory pressure evicts your B-tree's upper levels from cache. What happens to point-read latency, and why?
quiz.a: It rises. Normally only the leaf comes from disk because upper levels are cached. Without them, each lookup pays up to 3 to 5 disk reads instead of about one.

mcq.q: Why does a B-tree over billions of rows need only 3 to 5 levels?
options: Each page holds a few hundred keys
Rows are compressed before insertion
Leaf pages are linked in sorted order
The WAL indexes the most recent keys
mcq.why: High fan-out: each level multiplies reachable keys by a few hundred, so a handful of levels covers billions.

hook: A B-tree acknowledges your write before the changed page reaches disk. Why doesn't a crash lose it?
title: Log first, change in memory, flush the page later
body: Writing a changed page to its spot on disk is slow and random, so a B-tree defers it. First it appends a record to the **write-ahead log** (WAL), a sequential file; now the write is durable. Then it changes the leaf page in the **buffer pool**, the in-memory page cache. Much later, the whole dirty page is written back. If the machine crashes in between, replaying the log rebuilds the change.
takeaway: Durability lives in the log. The page on disk can catch up later.
deeper:
**Why the log works:** Appending to a sequential file is fast. Once the record is on disk, the change cannot be lost. If the machine dies before the dirty page is flushed, recovery replays the log and rebuilds it.

**Deferral pays twice:** Several changes to the same page can merge into one flush. But eventually the whole page, not just the changed bytes, goes back to its fixed location. Those locations are scattered across the tree, so flushes are random writes.

**The pattern everywhere:** Log-then-apply shows up across the stack. LSM-trees append to a commit log before acknowledging. DynamoDB acknowledges a write once a quorum of replicas has persisted the WAL record. Aurora goes furthest: the database sends only redo log records to storage and never ships data pages over the network. Storage builds the pages from the log itself.

quiz.q: A B-tree database acknowledged 1,000 writes, then lost power before flushing any dirty pages. After restart, how many writes survive, and how?
quiz.a: All 1,000. Each was in the on-disk WAL before the acknowledgment, so recovery replays the log and rebuilds the pages that never got flushed.

mcq.q: In a B-tree write, what makes the change durable before the page is flushed?
options: Appending a record to the write-ahead log
Changing the leaf page in the buffer pool
Splitting the page once it becomes full
Caching the upper tree levels in memory
mcq.why: The WAL is on disk and sequential. After a crash, replaying it rebuilds any dirty page that never reached disk.

hook: You change a 100-byte row. How many bytes does InnoDB actually write to disk?

predict.q: InnoDB, 16 KB pages. You change one 100-byte row. Roughly what write amplification for that page?
options: About 160×
About 2×
About 16×

title: A 100-byte change, a 16 KB write
body: A B-tree reads and writes whole pages, never single rows. So changing a 100-byte row can mean rewriting a 16 KB page: write amplification of about 160, plus the WAL record. InnoDB then adds a **doublewrite buffer** against **torn pages**, where a crash leaves a page half-written. That doubles page writes again. And the pages sit all over the tree, so the writes are random.
takeaway: B-trees charge by the page, not by the bytes you changed.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** 16,384 bytes written for a 100-byte change is roughly 160 times. The doublewrite buffer writes each page twice, so a torn page can be restored from the intact copy. Add the WAL record and small random updates climb well past 160.

**Randomness, the second cost:** Rows live in fixed pages across the tree. Updates to unrelated keys dirty pages everywhere. On spinning disks, every random write meant a seek, which hurt. On flash, random writes are fine but wasteful: the device still writes far more bytes than you changed, spending endurance and bandwidth.

**The contrast with LSM:** LSM write amplification can be high too, roughly one rewrite per level. But those writes are large, sequential and compressed. That difference is part of why Meta's move to MyRocks cut bytes written to flash by 75 percent.

quiz.q: Tables A and B get the same updates per second on 16 KB InnoDB pages. A's rows are 100 bytes, B's are 8 KB. Which has worse write amplification?
quiz.a: Table A. Each update rewrites a 16 KB page either way, so a 100-byte change is amplified about 160 times, an 8 KB change only about 2 times.

mcq.q: What does InnoDB's doublewrite buffer protect against?
options: Torn pages left half-written by a crash
Write amplification from page splits
Stale versions left behind by updates
Random seeks on spinning disks
mcq.why: A crash mid-write can leave a page partly written. Writing each page twice keeps an intact copy to restore from.

hook: Meta examined its InnoDB fleet and found a large slice of the disk holding nothing at all.

predict.q: Meta measured B-tree fragmentation across its InnoDB fleet. How much space did it waste?
options: 25 to 30 percent
2 to 3 percent
60 to 70 percent

title: Meta found 25-30% of its InnoDB space wasted
body: A B-tree page that fills up splits in two, and the halves are often left only 50 to 70 percent full. That leaves room for future inserts, but across millions of pages the gaps pile up. This empty space inside pages is **fragmentation**. Meta measured it across its InnoDB fleet: about 25 to 30 percent of space wasted. Those bytes cost SSD capacity and hold no live data. They also hurt compression.
takeaway: A page split buys cheap inserts with space you pay for forever.
deeper:
**Why splits leave gaps:** Splitting keeps the tree balanced and inserts cheap. Leaving free room in both halves stops the next insert from splitting again. Multiply by millions of pages and you get a fleetwide cost Meta could measure.

**Compression suffers too:** Each page is compressed on its own, free space included. Partly empty, independently compressed pages squeeze worse than a tightly packed, sorted file. The numbers: 200 GB of live data in a B-tree with pages about 70 percent full needs about 285 GB before compression. A leveled LSM needs about 1.1 times the compressed size.

**When it became decisive:** Meta moved its main database, UDB, to flash, and the bottleneck shifted from IOPS to capacity. InnoDB now had three space problems at once: index fragmentation, weak compression, and 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead. Those problems motivated MyRocks, a MySQL engine built on RocksDB.

quiz.q: A B-tree has about 30 percent free space inside its pages. Why does it also compress worse than a packed file holding the same rows?
quiz.a: Each page is compressed alone, gaps and all, in small units. A full, sorted file compresses long dense runs of similar data, so it shrinks much further.

mcq.q: Why are B-tree pages often left 50 to 70 percent full?
options: Full pages split into two partly filled halves
Compression reserves free space inside pages
The doublewrite buffer claims half of each page
Tombstones hold space until compaction runs
mcq.why: A full page splits into two partly filled halves. The leftover free room is fragmentation.

hook: Page-sized writes and 25-30% wasted space. So why do so many big systems still run B-trees underneath?
title: What B-trees buy: steady reads, no compaction storms
body: B-trees waste writes and space, yet many big systems keep one underneath. The return is worth it. Each key lives in exactly one place, so a point read costs about one disk read, every time. Range scans are cheap because leaves are sorted. Transaction and locking code has decades of maturity. And there are no **compaction storms**: no big background merge that can suddenly fight user traffic for the disk.
takeaway: Predictable beats efficient when a pager is watching your p99.
deeper:
**Background work you can reason about:** LSM engines periodically rewrite large amounts of data. If that falls behind, reads slow down and writes get throttled or stalled. A B-tree's background work is flushing dirty pages, plus vacuum in PostgreSQL. It is steadier and easier to plan for.

**Maturity keeps it underneath:** Many big systems build distribution layers on top of a B-tree engine. LinkedIn's Espresso uses MySQL/InnoDB on its storage nodes. Uber's Docstore replicates MySQL transactions with Raft. Vitess shards MySQL. DynamoDB's storage replicas keep data in a B-tree.

**Where it fits best:** Read-heavy OLTP and heavy transactions. Deletes are immediate, reads are predictable, and range scans are excellent. You pay with random I/O and 25 to 30 percent fragmentation, and for many workloads that is a fair price.

quiz.q: Your read-heavy payments database has a strict p99 target. A teammate proposes an LSM engine to save disk. What risk do you raise?
quiz.a: Compaction. If it falls behind, reads check more files and writes can stall, hurting p99. A B-tree gives steady one-read lookups and no compaction storms.

mcq.q: Which advantage do B-trees have over LSM-trees?
options: No background compaction competing with user traffic
Lower space amplification on flash storage
Sequential disk writes for every update
Tombstones that make deletes nearly free
mcq.why: B-trees update in place, so there is no big merge job. LSM compaction can cause latency spikes and write stalls.

hook: Random disk writes are slow. What if a database simply refused to do them, and paid the bill later?
title: LSM-trees: write sequentially now, merge later
body: Updating rows where they live means random disk writes. The **LSM-tree** (log-structured merge-tree), described by O'Neil and colleagues in 1996 and made famous by Google's Bigtable in 2006, refuses. Every write goes to memory and a sequential log. Full memory is flushed as one sorted file. Background **compaction** later merges files and drops old versions. Random writes become sequential, and the bill arrives later.
takeaway: An LSM-tree doesn't avoid work. It schedules it for later.
deeper:
**The write path:**
1. Append to the write-ahead log on disk.
2. Insert into the in-memory sorted memtable.
3. When the memtable fills, flush it as a Level 0 SSTable. Level 0 files may overlap.
4. Compaction merges them into Level 1, sorted with no overlap, then into levels each about 10 times bigger, until the last level holds most data.

**The read path runs backwards:** Check the memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit. A bloom filter per SSTable skips files that cannot hold the key.

**The deal:** Foreground writes are cheap and sequential. On-disk files are full and sorted, so they compress well. The deferred cost: compaction rewrites data several times, and reads may consult several files. LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra and Bigtable are all variations on managing that debt.

quiz.q: Your LSM database absorbs a big write burst without slowing down. Where does the cost of that burst show up afterward?
quiz.a: In compaction, which must rewrite that data several times, and in reads, which check more files until compaction catches up.

mcq.q: How does an LSM-tree turn random writes into sequential ones?
options: It buffers writes in memory and flushes whole sorted files
It sorts writes by page, then updates the pages in place
It spreads each write across all levels at once
It delays the write-ahead log until pages fill up
mcq.why: Writes collect in a memtable, backed by a sequential log, and reach disk as one sorted file instead of scattered page updates.

hook: An LSM-tree keeps your newest writes only in RAM. Pull the power cord. Why is nothing lost?
title: The memtable is fast. The log makes it safe.
body: Every LSM write lands in the **memtable**, an in-memory sorted structure, often a skip list. Inserting is fast and keys stay in order. But RAM vanishes in a crash. So before a write is acknowledged, it is also appended to the **write-ahead log**, or commit log, on disk. After a crash, the engine replays the log and rebuilds the memtable. No acknowledged write is lost, and neither step needed a random disk write.
takeaway: Memory gives you order. The log gives you survival.
deeper:
**Split duties:** The memtable provides ordering and fast lookups for recent data. The log provides durability through cheap sequential appends. The memtable is the only mutable piece; everything on disk is either appended or written once.

**When the memtable fills:** It has a size limit, for example 64 to 256 MB. When full, it is written out as one immutable, sorted SSTable. Its log segment is then no longer needed for recovery. Because the memtable is already sorted, the flush is one sequential write.

**The same shape at scale:** Each Bigtable tablet is an LSM-tree with a memtable, commit log and SSTables, all stored in GFS. When a tablet server dies, a replacement reopens the SSTables and replays the commit log. Cassandra borrowed the same commit log, memtable and SSTable design from Bigtable for its local storage.

quiz.q: An engineer turns off the commit log to speed up writes, reasoning that the memtable flushes every few minutes anyway. What breaks?
quiz.a: Anything acknowledged but not yet flushed lives only in RAM. A crash loses it, because there is no log to replay into the memtable.

mcq.q: Why does an LSM-tree append every write to a log before acknowledging it?
options: So a crash can replay it into the memtable
So compaction knows which files to merge
So bloom filters can index the new key
So reads can skip checking the memtable
mcq.why: The memtable lives in RAM. The on-disk log lets the engine rebuild it after a crash.

hook: An LSM-tree writes files it will never modify again, not for updates, not for deletes. Why is that a feature?
title: SSTables: sorted files that never change
body: When the memtable fills, for example at 64 to 256 MB, the LSM-tree writes it out as an **SSTable** (sorted string table). The file is immutable: never modified after it is written. Inside are data blocks of key-value pairs, an index block saying which block holds which key range, and usually a bloom filter that rules out absent keys. Updates and deletes never touch it. They show up as newer entries in newer files.
takeaway: A file that never changes can never be half-updated.
deeper:
**Why immutability is safe:** A file that never changes can be cached, copied and shared without locks. A crash can never leave it half-updated. Compaction simply writes fresh SSTables and retires the old ones.

**Why sorted pays:** The index block lets a reader jump straight to the one data block that might hold a key. Range scans read consecutive blocks. Sorted, packed data also compresses well, which is why a leveled LSM needs only about 1.1 times the compressed data size on disk.

**The architecture it unlocked:** Bigtable stores SSTables and commit logs in GFS, later Colossus, and never modifies them in place. So a tablet server holds no durable state. If it dies, another server reopens the same files. Replication and durability become the file system's job, not the database server's.

quiz.q: An SSTable is never modified. So how does an LSM-tree ever update or delete a key stored inside one?
quiz.a: It writes a newer value or a tombstone to a newer file. Reads see the newest entry first, and compaction later writes a fresh SSTable without the stale one.

mcq.q: What does an SSTable's index block do?
options: Maps key ranges to the data block that holds them
Rules out keys that are definitely not in the file
Records writes that are not yet flushed to disk
Tracks which files compaction should merge next
mcq.why: The index block points a reader to the one data block that could hold a key. Ruling keys out is the bloom filter's job.

hook: An LSM-tree never deletes or overwrites anything in place. So why doesn't its disk fill up forever?
title: Compaction: the background merge an LSM can't skip
body: An LSM-tree only ever adds files. Left alone, the file count grows forever, every read checks more of them, and stale versions fill the disk. **Compaction** is the fix: a background job that reads several SSTables, merges them in key order, throws away overwritten values and deleted keys, and writes fresh SSTables. It reclaims space and keeps read amplification bounded. It is also where LSM designs differ most.
takeaway: Every LSM write is a loan. Compaction is the repayment.
deeper:
**Cheap per byte:** Merging works like the merge step of merge sort. Each input is read sequentially and one sorted output is written. If a key appears in several inputs, only the newest version survives. If a key has a tombstone, the old value can finally be dropped.

**Still real work:** Each user byte may be rewritten several times as it moves down the levels. That is the main source of LSM write amplification. Compaction also takes disk bandwidth and CPU away from user traffic, and it can cause latency spikes.

**The strategies:**
1. Leveled (LevelDB and RocksDB default): low space, more rewriting.
2. Tiered (RocksDB universal, Cassandra size-tiered): fewer rewrites, more overlapping files.
3. FIFO: delete the oldest files, for data with a TTL.

Picking one is a workload decision, not a default to leave alone.

quiz.q: An LSM node's compaction threads are accidentally disabled for a week of steady writes. What do you expect to see?
quiz.a: File count keeps climbing, reads check ever more SSTables and slow down, and overwritten or deleted data fills the disk. Eventually the engine throttles writes.

mcq.q: During compaction, one key appears in three input SSTables. What is written to the output?
options: Only the newest version of the key
All three versions, in time order
The oldest version, as the canonical copy
A tombstone that hides the other two
mcq.why: Compaction keeps the newest value and discards overwritten ones. That is how it reclaims space.

hook: You delete a huge batch of rows from an LSM database, then check disk usage. It doesn't do what you expect.

predict.q: You delete 100 GB of rows from an LSM database. What happens to disk usage right away?
options: It rises slightly
It drops by about 100 GB
It stays exactly flat

title: In an LSM-tree, a delete is just another write
body: An LSM-tree never edits its files, so it cannot erase a key directly. A delete is written as a **tombstone**, a special record that says "this key is gone". It goes into the memtable and log like any other write, and reads that hit it treat the key as deleted. The old value stays on disk in older SSTables until compaction reaches it and drops both. So deleting data briefly adds bytes.
takeaway: An LSM delete adds bytes first and frees them later.
deeper:
**Why space doesn't come back:** The tombstone is a new record, so a delete briefly adds a little space. Bytes return only when compaction merges the tombstone with the files holding older versions.

**Why reads go newest first:** A lookup must meet the tombstone before the older value, or it would return deleted data. That is why reads check files newest to oldest and stop at the first hit. Delete-heavy workloads can leave many tombstones that reads must step over until compaction clears them.

**The B-tree contrast:** In a B-tree, a delete removes the row from its page in place. It is immediate. In an LSM-tree, deletes are tombstones until compaction.

**The escape hatch:** For data that expires by age, RocksDB's FIFO compaction and Cassandra's time-window strategy drop whole old files at once. There are no per-row tombstones to track.

quiz.q: A team deletes a user's rows from an LSM store and checks disk usage a minute later. It went up slightly. Is something broken?
quiz.a: No. Each delete wrote a tombstone, a new record. The old values stay in older SSTables until compaction merges them with the tombstones and drops both.

mcq.q: What is a tombstone in an LSM-tree?
options: A write that marks a key as deleted
A file that compaction has retired
A page left empty after a split
A log segment no longer needed
mcq.why: A delete can't edit immutable files, so it is written as a marker that hides older values until compaction removes them.

hook: One LSM key was updated three times, and each version sits in a different file. Which one does a read return?
title: LSM reads check newest first and stop at the first hit
body: In an LSM-tree, one key can live in several places: the memtable and any number of SSTables. A read checks the memtable first, then SSTables from newest to oldest, and stops at the first hit. Order matters because a newer file may hold an update or a tombstone that overrides older values. Looking in several places is **read amplification**. Two tools cut it: **bloom filters** skip files that definitely lack the key, and a **block cache** keeps hot data and index blocks in memory.
takeaway: In an LSM-tree, only the newest answer is the true one.
deeper:
**The worst case:** A missing key, or one living only in the last level. Without help, the reader probes every level. Leveled compaction limits this: SSTables inside one level never overlap, so a point read checks at most one file per level. Level 0 is the exception, since freshly flushed files may overlap.

**The helpers:** Bloom filters answer "definitely not here" for most wrong files. The block cache turns many remaining disk reads into memory reads for hot data and index blocks.

**Range scans are harder:** Bloom filters can't help, and a scan must merge several sorted runs from different files into one ordered stream. LSM scans are good but not excellent, next to a B-tree walking linked, sorted leaves.

**The catch:** When compaction falls behind, overlapping files pile up and read amplification climbs.

quiz.q: Someone patches an LSM engine to read SSTables oldest-first to speed up lookups of old keys. What bug appears?
quiz.a: Stale and deleted data comes back. An older file's value would be returned before the newer update or tombstone that should override it.

mcq.q: Why does an LSM read check SSTables from newest to oldest?
options: A newer file may override the key with an update or tombstone
Newer files are always smaller and cheaper to search
Older files lack bloom filters until compaction runs
The block cache only holds blocks from newer files
mcq.why: The first hit, searching newest first, is the current value. Older copies may be stale or deleted.

hook: Most files in an LSM-tree don't hold the key you want. How does a read avoid opening them all?

predict.q: A bloom filter uses about 10 bits per key. Roughly what false-positive rate does that buy?
options: About 1 percent
About 10 percent
About 0.001 percent

title: 10 bits per key: skip almost every wrong file

stat.label: false positives at about 10 bits per key

body: Most SSTables don't hold the key a read wants, but checking each one costs a disk read. A **bloom filter** avoids that: a small bit array per SSTable that answers "is this key definitely not here?" It says "definitely not" or "maybe". With about 10 bits per key, the false-positive rate is about 1 percent, so a point lookup skips almost every file that lacks the key.
takeaway: A filter that never lies about "no" can afford a wrong "maybe".
deeper:
**Why it is safe:** Bloom filters never give false negatives. If the filter says a key is absent, it is absent, so skipping the file is always correct. A false positive costs only one wasted block read, and at 1 percent that is cheap.

**The price:** Memory, about 10 bits per key per SSTable. A classic trade: spend space to cut read amplification.

**The blind spot:** A bloom filter hashes individual keys. It cannot answer "does this file hold any key between A and B?" So range scans still consult every file whose key range overlaps.

**RocksDB's patch:** Prefix bloom filters. If queries often scan all keys sharing a fixed prefix, such as one user's rows, the filter is built on that prefix. A scan can then skip files holding no keys with it. This is one of the features RocksDB added on top of LevelDB.

quiz.q: Your LSM service handles point lookups by order ID, plus a nightly scan of every order between two dates. Which do bloom filters speed up, and why only that one?
quiz.a: The point lookups. Bloom filters test individual hashed keys, so they skip files lacking a key, but cannot say whether any key in a date range exists.

mcq.q: A bloom filter answers "maybe" for a key in an SSTable. What does that mean?
options: The key may be present, so the file must be checked
The key is guaranteed to be in the file
The key was deleted and has a tombstone
The key's prefix exists but the key does not
mcq.why: A "maybe" can be a false positive, about 1 percent at 10 bits per key, so the file is read to confirm.

hook: An LSM-tree may hold hundreds of files. One compaction rule guarantees a point read opens only a few. Which?
title: Leveled compaction: at most one file per level
body: Leveled compaction, the default in LevelDB and RocksDB, sorts SSTables into levels L1, L2 and on. Each level is about 10 times bigger than the one above, the **size multiplier**. The key rule: inside one level, SSTables never overlap in key range. So a point read checks at most one file per level. When level N grows too big, the engine picks one file and merges it into the overlapping files of level N+1.
takeaway: No overlap inside a level means one file per level, at most.
deeper:
**The exception is Level 0:** Files flushed straight from the memtable may overlap. That is why a Level 0 backlog hurts reads so fast: every overlapping L0 file must be checked.

**Merges are incremental:** Compaction doesn't rewrite a whole level. It takes one file from level N and rewrites only the level N+1 files whose ranges overlap it. That keeps each job bounded. The catch: one file's worth of data can drag up to about 10 times its size of level N+1 data into the rewrite.

**The multiplier shapes everything:** With each level 10 times larger, most data ends up in the last level. Each byte is rewritten roughly once per level on its way down.

**The resulting profile:** Low space amplification and good reads, paid for with high write amplification. Leveled is the choice when reads and disk space matter more than write bandwidth.

quiz.q: A leveled LSM-tree has 4 overlapping Level 0 files and levels L1 to L6. Without bloom filters, how many SSTables does a point read check at worst?
quiz.a: About 10: all 4 overlapping Level 0 files, plus at most one file in each of L1 to L6, because files within those levels never overlap.

mcq.q: Under leveled compaction, what happens when level N grows too big?
options: One file merges into the overlapping files of level N+1
The whole level is rewritten into one large file
Its oldest files are deleted outright
It waits until enough similar-size files pile up
mcq.why: Leveled compaction is incremental: one file merges with only the overlapping N+1 files. Deleting oldest is FIFO; piling up is tiered.

hook: Stale copies of your data sit in every upper level of a leveled LSM-tree. Yet total overhead stays small. Why?

predict.q: Leveled LSM, each level 10× the one above. At most, how much extra space do stale upper-level copies add?
options: About 11 percent
About 50 percent
About 100 percent

title: Leveled LSM: about 11% extra space, lots of rewriting

stat.label: max overhead from stale upper-level copies

body: Leveled compaction keeps space tight. With a size multiplier of 10, about 90 percent of the data sits in the last level. Even if every upper-level copy were stale, together they would add only about 11 percent. The price is **write amplification**. Each byte is rewritten roughly once per level on the way down, and each merge may rewrite up to about 10 times its size of overlapping data.
takeaway: Leveled compaction buys a small disk with a busy one.
deeper:
**Where 11 percent comes from:** If each level is 10 times bigger than the one above, all upper levels together hold roughly one ninth as much as the last level. One ninth is about 11 percent. So leveled LSM space runs about 1.1 times the live, compressed data.

**Where the write cost comes from:** The same geometry. With several levels, a user byte may be rewritten once at each. The overlap between one file and the next level makes each merge expensive, and the total adds up.

**Who should use it:** Read-heavy data where space costs money.

**The failure mode:** A write spike can outrun compaction.
1. Level 0 and upper levels pile up overlapping files.
2. Stale versions take extra space.
3. Reads check more files and slow down.
4. Eventually the engine throttles writes.

quiz.q: A team lowers its leveled size multiplier from 10 to 4. Roughly what happens to the worst-case space overhead from upper levels?
quiz.a: It rises. Upper levels would hold about a third of the last level (1/4 + 1/16 + ...), so overhead grows from about 11 percent to about 33 percent.

mcq.q: Why does leveled compaction have high write amplification?
options: Each byte is rewritten about once per level
Every write is copied to all levels at once
Tombstones are rewritten on every read
Level 0 files are compressed twice over
mcq.why: Data moves down level by level, and each merge also rewrites overlapping data already in the next level.

hook: Leveled compaction rewrites every byte again and again. What if you let files pile up instead?
title: Tiered compaction: fewer rewrites, more files, more space
body: Leveled compaction keeps each level tidy, but it rewrites data often. **Tiered compaction**, RocksDB's universal style and Cassandra's size-tiered strategy, relaxes the rule. Several SSTables of similar size pile up in a tier. When there are enough, they all merge into one bigger file in the next tier. Each byte is rewritten fewer times, so write amplification drops. The bill moves to reads and space: overlapping files to check, duplicates that linger, and big merges that need room.
takeaway: Tiered compaction saves the disk's writes by spending its space.
deeper:
**Why reads suffer:** Files within a tier overlap in key range. A point lookup may check several files in the same tier, not one per level. It leans harder on bloom filters and caches.

**Why space suffers, twice:** Duplicate versions of a key live longer, because they are reconciled only when a whole tier merges. And a big merge may temporarily need double the space: the new combined file must be written before the inputs can be deleted. A disk sized for steady-state data can run out of room mid-compaction.

**Who should use it:** Write-heavy ingest. When the per-node write rate is high and SSD endurance or disk bandwidth is the constraint, rewriting each byte fewer times matters more than extra files and space.

**The ops rule:** Leave free disk for the largest merge, not just for the data.

quiz.q: A node on tiered compaction holds 400 GB of data on a 600 GB disk. A merge covering most of that data starts. What risk do you flag?
quiz.a: Running out of disk. A big tiered merge writes the new combined file before deleting its inputs, so it can briefly need about double the space.

mcq.q: Compared with leveled compaction, what does tiered compaction improve?
options: Write amplification
Read amplification
Space amplification
Point-read latency
mcq.why: Each byte is rewritten fewer times. Reads and space get worse because files overlap and duplicates linger.

hook: Your metrics expire after a week. Why would a database merge and rewrite them over and over before then?
title: For expiring data, skip merging and drop whole files
body: General compaction keeps merging old records down the levels, paying write amplification, even when they are about to expire. **FIFO compaction** in RocksDB skips that: it simply deletes the oldest files. It fits time-series or cache-like data with a **TTL** (time to live). Cassandra's time-window strategy exists for the same reason, grouping data by write time so whole windows drop once they expire. Neither wastes work rewriting data headed for the trash.
takeaway: Don't polish data you're about to throw away.
deeper:
**Why it is correct:** If data arrives roughly in time order and expires by age, the oldest file holds the oldest data. Dropping it whole is cheap and right. Deleting a file costs almost nothing next to rewriting it.

**It dodges tombstones too:** No per-row delete markers, no waiting for compaction to reconcile them. The engine removes an entire file and frees its space immediately.

**The limit:** It only works when writes and expiry are time-ordered. Data updated in place or deleted row by row doesn't fit. One old file may still hold live records, and dropping it would lose them.

**Where it shows up:** Messages and feeds are the classic case: write-heavy, time-ordered, with TTLs. They often live in Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase keyed by (user_id, time bucket).

quiz.q: A team moves user profiles, updated at random and never expiring, to FIFO compaction to save write bandwidth. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Live data gets deleted. FIFO drops the oldest files whole, and with random updates an old file can still hold the only copy of current records.

mcq.q: Which workload fits RocksDB's FIFO compaction?
options: Time-series data that expires after a fixed TTL
User profiles updated at random intervals
Payment records kept for many years
A social graph with frequent edge deletes
mcq.why: FIFO deletes the oldest files, which is only safe when data expires by age in write order.

hook: Most teams never touch their database's compaction setting. What are they silently agreeing to?
title: Compaction style is a workload decision, not a default
body: Engine defaults encode someone else's workload. So pick a compaction style by asking four questions. What is the write rate per node? What is the read pattern: point or range, fresh or old data? Is there a TTL? What is the SSD endurance budget? Then match. **Leveled** suits read-heavy data where space costs money. **Tiered** suits write-heavy ingest. **FIFO** or time-window suits data that expires.
takeaway: A default is someone else's workload, frozen into config.
deeper:
**Each question maps to a cost:** Write rate and SSD endurance set how much write amplification you can afford. A heavily written node can wear its flash quickly under leveled compaction. The read pattern sets how much read amplification you can tolerate. Point reads on fresh data are served well by the memtable and bloom filters. Range scans over old data depend on how many overlapping files exist. A TTL says most data will be thrown away, so rewriting it is waste.

**Wrong is not just slower:** If compaction can't keep up with the write rate, Level 0 fills, reads slow down, and RocksDB throttles or stalls writes. A tuning mistake becomes an outage-shaped latency problem.

**Why it matters at scale:** One setting multiplies across thousands of nodes. Decide it explicitly, and revisit it when the workload changes.

quiz.q: Service A is a read-heavy product catalog on expensive disk. Service B is a firehose of sensor writes kept for 7 days. Pick a compaction style for each.
quiz.a: A: leveled, for low space and good reads. B: FIFO or time-window, since data expires by age and dropping whole old files avoids rewriting it.

mcq.q: Which workload is the best fit for tiered compaction?
options: Write-heavy ingest limited by disk bandwidth
Read-heavy data where disk space is expensive
Time-series data that expires after a TTL
Range scans over old, rarely changed data
mcq.why: Tiered rewrites each byte fewer times, saving write bandwidth and endurance at the cost of reads and space.

hook: Store the same 200 GB of rows in a B-tree and in an LSM-tree. The disk bills are nowhere near equal.

predict.q: 200 GB of live rows in a B-tree whose pages are about 70% full. Roughly how much disk before compression?
options: About 285 GB
About 200 GB
About 600 GB

title: Same 200 GB: B-tree 285 GB raw, LSM 1.1× compressed
body: Take 1 billion message-metadata rows of 200 bytes: 200 GB of live data. A B-tree with pages about 70 percent full needs about 285 GB before compression. It compresses poorly, because each page is compressed alone with its free space inside. A **leveled LSM-tree** needs about 1.1 times the compressed size, because SSTables are packed full and sorted. Its write amplification is real, roughly one rewrite per level, but those writes are large, sequential and compressed.
takeaway: When capacity is the bottleneck, the tightest packer wins.
deeper:
**The 285:** It is simply 200 GB spread over pages that are only about 70 percent full.

**Meta saw it in production:** Moving its main MySQL database from compressed InnoDB to MyRocks (MySQL on RocksDB) cut instance size by 62.3 percent and bytes written to flash by 75 percent. Smaller instances mean fewer servers and SSDs. Fewer bytes written means longer SSD life.

**Why the trade paid off:** The bottleneck had moved. On spinning disks, random IOPS were scarce and a B-tree's predictable reads were worth a lot. On flash, capacity became the expensive resource. Once capacity binds, the engine that packs and compresses best wins, even with more background rewriting.

**Read write amplification carefully:** An LSM rewrites each byte several times, yet total flash writes still fell. B-trees write whole pages for tiny changes, write the free space inside them, and InnoDB's doublewrite buffer adds more.

quiz.q: Your fleet moved from spinning disks to flash and now runs out of disk space long before it runs out of IOPS. Which engine family becomes more attractive, and why?
quiz.a: LSM. Capacity is now the bottleneck, and LSM files are packed full, sorted and compress well, so the same data needs far less disk.

mcq.q: Why does a B-tree compress worse than a leveled LSM-tree?
options: Each page is compressed alone, free space included
B-trees store their rows in no particular order
B-tree pages are too large to compress well
LSM-trees skip writing a write-ahead log
mcq.why: Partly full pages compressed one at a time shrink poorly. LSM SSTables are full and sorted, so they compress far better.

hook: Your benchmark says the LSM engine writes blazingly fast. Run it for a day and the picture changes. Why?
title: "LSM is always faster for writes" forgets compaction
body: An LSM write only touches the memtable and a sequential log, so the foreground cost is low. That is where the myth starts. **Compaction** is real work that must keep pace. If it falls behind, Level 0 fills with overlapping files, reads slow down because they check more files, and RocksDB throttles or stalls writes. The fix: size disk bandwidth for compaction, not just for user writes.
takeaway: An LSM write is cheap until the compaction bill comes due.
deeper:
**Why benchmarks lie:** In a run of a few minutes, an LSM engine absorbs writes very fast because compaction hasn't caught up with the backlog yet. A benchmark that ends early measures the loan, not the repayment. In steady state, every user byte must eventually be rewritten roughly once per level. Sustained write capacity is disk bandwidth divided by total write amplification.

**The symptoms, in order:**
1. Overlapping files pile up in Level 0 and upper levels.
2. Space amplification rises as stale versions go unmerged.
3. Read latency rises because lookups check more files.
4. RocksDB applies backpressure, slowing or stalling incoming writes.

**Plan for it:** Treat compaction as a first-class workload. Budget disk bandwidth, CPU and SSD endurance for it, alongside user traffic.

quiz.q: An LSM node's disk sustains 200 MB/s of writes, and total write amplification is 10. A ten-minute load test hit 80 MB/s of user writes. Is that sustainable?
quiz.a: No. Steady state needs about 800 MB/s of disk writes (80 × 10). The test ended before compaction caught up; sustained capacity is about 20 MB/s.

mcq.q: Compaction falls behind during a write spike. What happens first?
options: Overlapping files pile up in Level 0
RocksDB drops the oldest SSTables
Tombstones are converted into updates
The memtable spills into a B-tree
mcq.why: Flushes arrive faster than merges, so Level 0 overlap grows. Slower reads and write stalls follow.

hook: Two engine families, eight properties. Which wins on deletes, which on space, which on range scans?
title: B-tree vs LSM: who wins each row of the table
body: Side by side, the two families split cleanly. **B-trees** update pages in place with random I/O. They give predictable reads of about one disk read, excellent range scans and immediate deletes, but lose 25 to 30 percent of space to fragmentation. **LSM-trees** append with sequential I/O. With leveled compaction they pack data to about 1.1 times, but reads may check several files and deletes stay tombstones until compaction. B-trees fit read-heavy OLTP; LSM-trees fit write-heavy, large, flash, cost-sensitive data.
takeaway: B-trees sell predictability. LSM-trees sell density. Buy what you're short of.
deeper:
**Write path:** B-tree write amplification is high for small random writes, because every change is page-sized. LSM write amplification is moderate to high, but sequential and compressible.

**Background work:** B-trees flush pages and, in PostgreSQL, run vacuum. LSM-trees run compaction, which can cause latency spikes.

**Read path:** A B-tree scan walks sorted leaf pages. An LSM scan must merge several sorted runs: good, not excellent. Bloom filters help LSM point reads but not scans.

**The RUM trade in action:** B-trees buy predictable reads, scans and simple deletes, paying with writes and space. LSM-trees buy sequential writes and compact storage, paying with read effort and background work.

**Best fit is a starting point:** Meta's UDB moved from one column to the other when flash changed its bottleneck from IOPS to capacity. The trigger was the hardware.

quiz.q: Workload 1 needs deletes to take effect on disk immediately. Workload 2 is a huge, write-heavy dataset where disk cost dominates. Which engine suits each?
quiz.a: Workload 1: B-tree, since deletes are immediate while LSM tombstones wait for compaction. Workload 2: LSM, for sequential writes and about 1.1× space.

mcq.q: Which property does the B-tree win in the comparison?
options: Predictable point-read latency
Low space amplification
Sequential write I/O
Compressible writes
mcq.why: A B-tree read costs about one disk read; LSM reads may check several files. LSM-trees win the other three.

hook: Facebook forked a Google storage library in 2012. It now runs under a startling number of other databases.
title: RocksDB: an engine you link in, not a server you run
body: Every company wanted a fast, crash-safe LSM engine for flash, and nobody wanted to spend years writing one. **RocksDB** started at Facebook in 2012 as a fork of Google's LevelDB, tuned for fast flash and server workloads. The crucial choice: it is a C++ library, not a server. You link it into your own process, and it manages LSM storage on that one machine. No network protocol, no replication, no opinions about the layers above.
takeaway: Build the part that differs. Link the part that doesn't.
deeper:
**What it added to LevelDB:** Each feature targets a production problem.
1. Multi-threaded compaction, so many cores keep up with high write rates on flash.
2. Several compaction styles (leveled, universal, FIFO) to match the workload.
3. Column families: separate groups of data with their own settings in one database.
4. Prefix bloom filters for scans over fixed key prefixes.
5. Rate limiters that cap background I/O so compaction doesn't starve users.

**Why the library form won:** With no replication or cluster management of its own, RocksDB imposes nothing on those layers. A company builds whatever distributed system it needs and uses RocksDB purely as the single-node engine.

**The catch:** The many tuning knobs make it adaptable, but defaults are rarely optimal. Compaction style and its friends stay workload decisions you own.

quiz.q: Your team needs a replicated key-value store with custom sharding. Why might you link RocksDB instead of adopting a full database server?
quiz.a: RocksDB handles only the hard single-node part, a crash-safe LSM engine. It imposes no networking, replication or sharding, so you build those your way on top.

mcq.q: What is RocksDB?
options: A C++ LSM library linked into your own process
A distributed database server with built-in replication
A B-tree engine that replaced InnoDB in MySQL
A Go LSM engine written for CockroachDB
mcq.why: RocksDB is an embeddable single-node library. Pebble is the Go engine; MyRocks puts RocksDB under MySQL.

hook: MySQL at Meta, TiDB, YugabyteDB, LinkedIn's Venice, an Instagram Cassandra fork. What sits under all of them?
title: RocksDB: the engine inside everyone else's engine
body: Writing a correct, fast, crash-safe LSM engine takes years. Replication, sharding and query layers genuinely differ by company; the single-node engine doesn't need to. So companies build their own distributed layer and reuse **RocksDB** underneath. Meta runs it in MyRocks, ZippyDB and many internal services. LinkedIn's Venice uses it on storage nodes. TiDB's TiKV and YugabyteDB's DocDB are built on it. Instagram built **Rocksandra**, Cassandra on a RocksDB engine.
takeaway: Companies compete on replication and sharding, not on the single-node engine.
deeper:
**Different reasons, same engine:** Meta wanted MySQL compatibility with better space efficiency, so it put RocksDB under MySQL. TiKV and DocDB put it beneath their own Raft replication. Instagram's reason was latency: Cassandra's Java storage engine suffered garbage-collection pauses that showed up as tail latency. Moving storage into RocksDB's C++ code cut that source of pauses.

**The counterexample:** CockroachDB used RocksDB, then replaced it with Pebble, written in Go. But Pebble is still an LSM engine inspired by RocksDB. Even a company that leaves RocksDB keeps its design.

**Why reuse is rational:** Each company's replication, sharding and query layers reflect its own consistency needs, geography and operations. That is where real differentiation lives. The bytes-on-one-disk problem is shared, and solving it once lets everyone spend their years on the layers above.

quiz.q: Instagram's Cassandra clusters showed tail-latency spikes caused by the storage engine, not the distribution layer. What was the cause, and what did Instagram do?
quiz.a: Java garbage-collection pauses in Cassandra's storage engine. Instagram built Rocksandra, swapping that engine for RocksDB and keeping Cassandra's distributed layer.

mcq.q: Which system replaced RocksDB with a different LSM engine?
options: CockroachDB, with Pebble
TiDB, with TiFlash
YugabyteDB, with DocDB
Venice, with Da Vinci
mcq.why: CockroachDB swapped RocksDB for Pebble, a Go LSM inspired by RocksDB. DocDB runs on RocksDB; TiFlash is a columnar replica; Da Vinci is a client.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Google stored web pages under backwards URLs like com.cnn.www. Why would anyone flip a URL around?
title: Bigtable reversed URLs to keep each site together
body: Google needed to store petabytes of structured data, from the web crawl to Google Earth and Analytics, across thousands of machines. Relational databases of the time couldn't scale that far. **Bigtable** (2006) is a sparse, sorted, multi-dimensional map: (row key, column family:qualifier, timestamp) maps to a value. Rows are sorted by row key. So storing pages under reversed URLs like com.cnn.www puts every page from one site side by side.
takeaway: In a sorted store, the row key is your query plan.
deeper:
**Each dimension earns its place:** Sparse means a row needn't have every column, so missing cells cost nothing. Column families group related columns; qualifiers name columns inside a family. The timestamp lets one cell hold several versions.

**Sorting is the big bet:** It makes scans over adjacent keys cheap and lets the table split into contiguous ranges.

**Why reversing works:** www.cnn.com and money.cnn.com sort far apart. com.cnn.www and com.cnn.money sort together. One range scan reads a whole site, and those rows tend to land on the same server.

**The catch:** Key design becomes the application's job. Sorted keys mean sequential keys pile onto one range, and a hot row range can overload one tablet server until the tablet splits. That is why a timestamp or auto-increment ID makes a dangerous leading key in any range-partitioned store.

quiz.q: You store app events in Bigtable with the timestamp as the row key. One tablet server is overloaded while others idle. Why, and what does the reversed-URL trick suggest?
quiz.a: Rows sort by key, so every new event lands at the end of one range on one server. As with reversed URLs, redesign the key, for example prefix or reverse it, to spread writes.

mcq.q: What does Bigtable's data model map to a value?
options: Row key, column family:qualifier and timestamp
Table name, primary key and version number
Partition key, sort key and region
Document ID, field path and schema version
mcq.why: Bigtable is a sparse, sorted map keyed by row key, column family:qualifier and timestamp.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: One master coordinates thousands of Bigtable servers. Why doesn't it collapse under all that traffic?
title: Bigtable's master never touches client data
body: A single coordinator for thousands of servers sounds like a bottleneck. Bigtable keeps its master off the data path. Tables split into **tablets**, contiguous row ranges of about 100 to 200 MB. Each tablet server serves roughly ten to a thousand of them. The master only assigns tablets, balances load and garbage-collects files. **Chubby**, a Paxos-based lock service, holds the master lock, the root of tablet locations and server liveness.
takeaway: Keep the coordinator on the control path, never the data path.
deeper:
**How a client finds data:** It follows tablet location metadata whose root lives in Chubby, then talks straight to the tablet server. The master handles only low-volume control work.

**Why Chubby:** Some decisions must be strongly consistent. The master lock ensures only one master acts at a time. Liveness records let the master see which tablet servers are alive and reassign tablets from dead ones. Because Chubby runs Paxos, these decisions survive single machine failures.

**Growth without resharding:** Tables start as one tablet and split as they grow. Automatic splitting is the most operator-friendly way to reshard, but a system must be built for it from the start.

**The limit:** Splitting reacts to growth. A sudden hot row range can overload one server until its tablet splits.

**Inside each tablet:** An LSM-tree: memtable, commit log and SSTables, with the files in GFS.

quiz.q: Bigtable's master is down for a minute. Can clients keep reading and writing tablets that are already assigned? Why?
quiz.a: Largely yes. Client data never flows through the master; clients find tablets via metadata rooted in Chubby and talk directly to tablet servers. Assignment and balancing pause.

mcq.q: What does Chubby store for Bigtable?
options: The master lock, the tablet location root and server liveness
The SSTables and commit logs for every tablet
A cache of hot rows that speeds up reads
The schema and column families of each table
mcq.why: Chubby is a Paxos lock service for coordination state. Tablet data files live in GFS.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: A Bigtable tablet server dies under load. Nothing is copied off it, and nothing is lost. How?
title: Bigtable servers hold no data worth losing
body: Each Bigtable tablet keeps its commit log and SSTables in GFS, Google's distributed file system, later succeeded by Colossus. The tablet server itself holds no durable state. If it dies, another server reopens the same files, replays the commit log to rebuild the memtable, and keeps serving. That split is Bigtable's key idea: a **stateless serving layer** over a shared, replicated file system. Replication and durability are the file system's job; Bigtable only indexes and serves.
takeaway: Put durability in one layer and serving in another. Failures get boring.
deeper:
**Each half gets simpler:** The file system focuses on keeping bytes safe across machines. Bigtable focuses on the data model, sorting, caching and serving. It never implements its own replication protocol.

**Recovery is reassignment, not copying:**
1. A tablet server fails.
2. The master assigns its tablets to other servers.
3. They open the SSTables already in GFS.
4. They replay the commit log to rebuild the memtable.

No data comes off the dead machine, because none lived only there.

**Immutability makes it natural:** SSTables never change, so whichever server owns the tablet right now can read them safely.

**The pattern spreads:** Spanner keeps its tablets' files and WAL on Colossus. Aurora splits its database engine from a replicated storage service, though Aurora ships redo log records rather than files.

quiz.q: Your team builds a Bigtable-style store but keeps each server's commit log on local disk to cut latency. What have you given up?
quiz.a: Stateless failover. If that server dies, its unflushed writes live only on its disk, so another server can't just reopen shared files and replay the log.

mcq.q: When a Bigtable tablet server dies, how does another server take over its tablets?
options: It reopens the files in GFS and replays the commit log
It copies the SSTables off the dead server's disk
It rebuilds the tablets from snapshots in Chubby
It waits for the dead server to restart and resync
mcq.why: Durable state lives in replicated GFS/Colossus, so the new server reopens the files and replays the log.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: By 2006 Bigtable ran more than sixty Google products, yet couldn't update two rows atomically. Why?
title: Bigtable bought scale with one-row transactions
body: Scaling across thousands of machines forced Bigtable to give things up. It offers **single-row transactions** only: one row changes atomically, but several rows can't change together. It has no secondary indexes, so you find data efficiently only by row key. Hot row ranges can overload one tablet server until the tablet splits. Even so, the 2006 paper reported Bigtable in use by more than sixty Google products. HBase is the open-source copy of the design.
takeaway: Every feature you drop is coordination you never have to scale.
deeper:
**Why one row:** Cross-row transactions need coordination between tablets, possibly on different servers. That is exactly the distributed work that makes systems hard to scale. Keeping atomicity to one row keeps every operation local to one tablet server.

**Why no secondary indexes:** Query design moves to the application. Teams pick row keys that match their access patterns, like reversed URLs, or maintain their own index tables.

**Why hot ranges hurt:** Range partitioning puts sequential or popular keys on one tablet, and splitting helps only after the split happens.

**What came next:** Google's ads team (F1) needed SQL, strong consistency and global replication for money data. Bigtable couldn't give it, which led to Spanner in 2012. Meanwhile HBase brought Bigtable's design to open source, and Cassandra borrowed its LSM storage layout.

quiz.q: A payments team wants to debit one account and credit another in one Bigtable operation, with the rows on different tablets. What's the problem, and what did Google build for this need?
quiz.a: Bigtable is atomic only within one row, so the two updates can't commit together. Google built Spanner for cross-row transactions, SQL and strong consistency on money data.

mcq.q: Which capability was missing from Bigtable?
options: Transactions across multiple rows
Sorted range scans by row key
Timestamped versions within a cell
Automatic tablet splits as tables grow
mcq.why: Bigtable offered single-row atomicity only. Cross-row transactions came later with Spanner.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Two-phase commit's weak spot: the coordinator crashes and everyone waits. How did Spanner remove it?
title: Spanner: two-phase commit where every party is Paxos
body: Google's ads team (F1) needed what Bigtable lacked: SQL, strong consistency and global replication for money data. **Spanner** (2012) splits data into tablets stored in B-tree-like files plus a WAL on Colossus. Each tablet's replicas form a **Paxos group** with a long-lived leader, and a majority, often across zones or regions, must accept every write. Transactions spanning groups use two-phase commit, and each participant, coordinator included, is itself a Paxos group. No single machine can stall a commit.
takeaway: Replicate the coordinator, and two-phase commit stops being fragile.
deeper:
**The 2PC fix:** In classic two-phase commit, a crashed coordinator can leave participants stuck waiting. In Spanner the coordinator is a replicated Paxos group, so another replica takes over with the transaction state intact.

**Data moves in directories:** A directory is a set of keys sharing a common prefix, and it is the unit that moves between Paxos groups. A 50 MB directory moves in a few seconds, so Spanner can rebalance load or bring data closer to users.

**Keeping transactions local:** Directories and interleaved tables keep related data, such as one customer's rows, together. Most transactions then stay inside one group.

**The ambition:** The 2012 paper describes a design meant to scale to millions of machines across hundreds of datacenters and trillions of rows. It is also sold as Cloud Spanner. Its most famous piece, TrueTime, makes all of this appear to follow one global order.

quiz.q: A Spanner transaction touches three Paxos groups. Midway, the machine leading the coordinator group crashes. Why don't the other participants hang?
quiz.a: The coordinator is itself a Paxos group, so another replica becomes leader and continues the commit with the transaction state intact.

mcq.q: In Spanner, what unit moves between Paxos groups to rebalance data?
options: Directories, sets of keys with a common prefix
Tablets, fixed 100 to 200 MB row ranges
Regions, managed by a central placement driver
Vindexes, which map columns to shards
mcq.why: Spanner moves directories; a 50 MB one moves in a few seconds. Regions with a placement driver are TiDB; vindexes are Vitess.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Every server clock is wrong by an unknown amount. How do you order transactions across continents anyway?
title: TrueTime: a clock that says how wrong it might be
body: Server clocks drift by unknown amounts, so timestamps from different machines can't be safely compared. Spanner's **TrueTime** API returns an interval, [earliest, latest], guaranteed to contain the true time. GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each datacenter keep it narrow. In production the uncertainty, **epsilon**, ran in a sawtooth from about 1 to 7 ms, and was about 4 ms most of the time.
takeaway: An error you can measure is an error you can wait out.
deeper:
**Unknown becomes bounded:** If two intervals don't overlap, their order is certain. If they overlap, Spanner knows it must wait for the uncertainty to pass.

**Why a sawtooth:** Uncertainty grows as local clocks drift between synchronizations with the GPS and atomic time masters, then drops back when they resync.

**Why small epsilon matters:** Commit wait is set by the uncertainty. The leader waits it out on every write, so a bigger epsilon would slow every write directly.

**The barrier to copying:** The hardware is what others lack. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB copy Spanner's design of ranges replicated by consensus, but without atomic clocks they rely on hybrid logical clocks and bounded clock skew. They sometimes retry reads that fall in an uncertainty window.

quiz.q: Suppose TrueTime's epsilon grew from about 4 ms to 40 ms. What would happen to Spanner write latency, and why?
quiz.a: It would rise by tens of milliseconds. The leader waits out the uncertainty before exposing each commit, so a wider interval means a longer commit wait on every write.

mcq.q: What does TrueTime return instead of a single timestamp?
options: An interval guaranteed to contain the true time
A logical counter combined with physical time
A timestamp issued by a central oracle
The median of all datacenter clocks
mcq.why: TrueTime returns [earliest, latest]. Hybrid logical clocks belong to CockroachDB and YugabyteDB; a central oracle is TiDB.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: T1 commits on one continent. T2 starts moments later on another. What stops T2 getting an earlier timestamp?
title: Commit wait: Spanner waits out the clock, then answers
body: Clocks disagree, so a later transaction on another machine could get a smaller timestamp than one already committed. Spanner prevents that with **commit wait**. The leader picks a commit timestamp, then waits out TrueTime's uncertainty before making the write visible. After the wait, that timestamp is in the past on every clock. The result is **external consistency**: if T1 commits before T2 starts, T1's timestamp is smaller, as if one global clock existed.
takeaway: Spanner doesn't beat clock uncertainty. It waits it out.
deeper:
**What would break without it:** A transaction could commit with a timestamp another machine's clock hasn't reached yet. A later transaction there could then receive a smaller timestamp, and the database's order would contradict real time.

**The payoff for reads:** Because timestamps match real-time order, any timestamp is a consistent snapshot of the whole database. A read at timestamp T needs no locks: everything committed before T is visible, nothing after it is. Large consistent reads, backups and analytics get cheap.

**The bill:** Every write pays a Paxos round trip plus a few milliseconds of commit wait. Cross-region Paxos groups push writes to tens of milliseconds. You buy correctness with latency and special hardware.

**Why Google paid it:** The customer was money data in the ads system, where correctness was the whole point.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes skipping commit wait to shave a few milliseconds off Spanner writes. What anomaly could users then see?
quiz.a: A transaction that starts after another commits could get a smaller timestamp, so snapshots would show events out of real-time order, breaking external consistency.

mcq.q: What does external consistency guarantee?
options: If T1 commits before T2 starts, T1 has the smaller timestamp
Every replica applies each write within 7 ms of the others
Reads always go to the Paxos leader of each group
Two-phase commit never blocks on a failed coordinator
mcq.why: Commit wait makes timestamp order match real-time order, as if there were one global clock.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: CockroachDB and YugabyteDB copied Spanner's design almost whole. One piece they couldn't copy was hardware.
title: Spanner's bill: tens of ms per write, plus atomic clocks
body: Spanner's correctness has a price. Every write pays a Paxos round trip to a majority of replicas plus a few milliseconds of commit wait. When a Paxos group spans regions, writes cost tens of milliseconds. You buy correctness with latency and special hardware. Open systems like CockroachDB and YugabyteDB copy the rest of the design, ranges replicated by consensus plus distributed transactions, but without atomic clocks. They use **hybrid logical clocks** and bounded clock skew instead.
takeaway: Strong consistency is paid for in round trips. Somebody always pays.
deeper:
**Why the latency is physics:** A majority of replicas across regions means at least one long-distance round trip per write. Commit wait adds roughly the clock uncertainty on top. Apps on Spanner accept slower writes in exchange for never seeing ordering anomalies.
