**What the copies keep:** A sorted key space split into ranges, each range replicated by consensus, and a transaction layer coordinating multi-range writes.

**What they swap:** Hybrid logical clocks combine physical time with logical counters and assume skew between machines stays under a configured bound. When a read's timestamp falls inside that uncertainty window, they may have to retry it.

**A third path:** TiDB uses a central timestamp oracle in its Placement Driver. Simple and correct, but it adds a round trip to one service.

**Scale claim:** Spanner was designed for millions of machines, hundreds of datacenters and trillions of rows (2012 paper), and is sold as Cloud Spanner.

quiz.q: Your CockroachDB cluster occasionally retries a read for no obvious reason. Which design difference from Spanner explains it?
quiz.a: Without atomic clocks, it uses hybrid logical clocks with bounded skew. A read whose timestamp falls in the clock uncertainty window may be retried; Spanner relies on TrueTime instead.

mcq.q: Why do Spanner writes across regions cost tens of milliseconds?
options: Each needs a cross-region Paxos majority plus commit wait
Each must reach every replica in every region
TrueTime queries GPS satellites on every commit
Two-phase commit runs on every single-row write
mcq.why: A majority of cross-region replicas must accept the write, then commit wait adds a few milliseconds of clock uncertainty.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Amazon picked one action that must never fail, even mid-outage: adding an item to your shopping cart.
title: Dynamo: built so the cart is always writable
body: In 2007, Amazon described **Dynamo**, an internal key-value store for things like the shopping cart. The goal was "always writable": a customer must be able to add to the cart even during failures. Keys spread over nodes with **consistent hashing** and virtual nodes. Each application tuned its quorum (N, R, W): N replicas, R needed to read, W needed to write. A common setting was (3, 2, 2). The SLA was measured at the 99.9th percentile, for example 300 ms.
takeaway: Decide what must never fail, then let everything else bend.
deeper:
**Consistent hashing:** Nodes and keys sit on a hash ring. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys next to it, not everything. Virtual nodes give each machine many ring positions, spreading load evenly and letting bigger machines take bigger shares.

**Why (3, 2, 2) works:** Three replicas; a write succeeds when two acknowledge; a read consults two. Since R plus W exceeds N, a read normally overlaps at least one replica that saw the latest write. Lower R or W and you trade that overlap for availability and latency.

**The 99.9th percentile:** Measuring the tail instead of the average means nearly every customer, not just a typical one, gets a fast answer.

**Distribution, not storage:** Local engines were pluggable (Berkeley DB, MySQL). Dynamo was leaderless and eventually consistent, and Cassandra and Riak copied the model.

quiz.q: A Dynamo-style store runs N = 3. To cut latency, a team sets W = 1 and R = 1. What guarantee did they give up?
quiz.a: Read-write overlap. With R + W = 2, not above N = 3, a read can hit only replicas that missed the latest write, so stale reads become normal.

mcq.q: With Dynamo's (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2), why does a read usually see the latest write?
options: R + W exceeds N, so read and write sets overlap
A leader replica serves every read request
Vector clocks block reads until writes finish
Hinted handoff copies each write to all nodes
mcq.why: Two read replicas and two write replicas out of three must share at least one node.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: During a network split, you add a book on one replica and a lamp on another. What does your cart show?
title: Dynamo kept writing through failures, then merged carts
body: Always writable means accepting writes even when replicas are down or cut off. Dynamo used a **sloppy quorum** with **hinted handoff**: if a replica is down, another node holds the write temporarily and hands it back later. That lets different nodes accept conflicting writes, so Dynamo tracked versions with **vector clocks** to detect conflicts. The application merged them, for example by taking the union of two carts. Merkle trees drove anti-entropy repair between drifting replicas.
takeaway: If you never refuse a write, someday you must merge two truths.
deeper:
**Availability over agreement:** A strict quorum would reject writes when too many of a key's home replicas were down. A sloppy quorum counts whatever healthy nodes are available, so the cart stays writable. The cost: replicas temporarily disagree.

**Vector clocks:** They record which node has seen which updates. The system can tell whether one version supersedes another or whether both diverged concurrently. Dynamo didn't pick a winner; it handed conflicting versions to the application.

**The cart merge:** A union keeps any item added on either side. The catch: a deleted item can occasionally reappear.

**Merkle trees:** Each replica builds a hash tree over its key ranges. Matching roots mean matching data. Different roots? Walk down the tree to the exact keys that differ, without shipping everything. Anti-entropy repair still matters: Uber's 2023 Cassandra post named slow repair a main pain point.

quiz.q: During a split, one Dynamo replica records "remove lamp" from a cart while another records "add book". After a union merge, what might the customer see, and why?
quiz.a: Both the book and the lamp. Vector clocks flag the versions as concurrent, and a union keeps every item present in either version, so the removed lamp can reappear.

mcq.q: What does hinted handoff do in Dynamo?
options: Another node holds a down replica's write, then hands it back
Vector clocks pick the newest write automatically
Merkle trees copy all data to a recovering node
The leader forwards writes to followers in order
mcq.why: It keeps writes flowing while a replica is down; the temporary holder returns the data once the replica recovers.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: DynamoDB shares a name with Amazon's 2007 Dynamo. Assume it works the same way and you'll be wrong.
title: DynamoDB is not Dynamo: leaders, Paxos, B-trees
body: The names cause real confusion in design reviews. **DynamoDB** (launched 2012, described in a 2022 USENIX ATC paper) kept Dynamo's name and its goal of predictable performance, but changed the core design. Tables split into partitions, each with three replicas in three Availability Zones. The replicas form a **Multi-Paxos** group, and only the leader accepts writes and strongly consistent reads. So DynamoDB is leader-based and strongly consistent within a partition, not leaderless and eventually consistent.
takeaway: Same name, opposite design. Check the architecture, not the label.
deeper:
**Writes:** Dynamo let any replica accept a write, detected conflicts with vector clocks, and made applications merge them. DynamoDB orders every write through one leader per partition via Multi-Paxos, so there are no conflicting versions to merge.

**Reads:** DynamoDB serves strongly consistent reads from the leader, and eventually consistent reads per request if you ask for them.

**Storage:** Dynamo used pluggable engines like Berkeley DB or MySQL. Each DynamoDB storage replica holds a write-ahead log and a B-tree.

**Operations:** DynamoDB is a multi-tenant managed service with admission control, not an internal store run by one team.

**The common error:** Crediting DynamoDB with sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and app-level merging. Those belong to the 2007 design and its descendants, Cassandra and Riak. DynamoDB is leader-based, with Multi-Paxos per partition.

quiz.q: A colleague says DynamoDB apps must merge conflicting versions, like the old Dynamo shopping cart. How do you correct them?
quiz.a: DynamoDB has one Multi-Paxos leader per partition that orders all writes, so conflicting versions don't arise. App-level merging belonged to the leaderless 2007 Dynamo.

mcq.q: How does DynamoDB replicate a partition?
options: A Multi-Paxos group with one leader
A leaderless ring with sloppy quorums
Chain replication through three nodes
Raft over MySQL in each zone
mcq.why: Each partition's three replicas form a Multi-Paxos group; only the leader takes writes. Leaderless rings were Dynamo; Raft over MySQL is Docstore.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: A DynamoDB storage node dies, and rebuilding a full replica is slow. How is the write quorum back in seconds?
title: DynamoDB acks on the log, heals with log replicas
body: A request router authenticates each request, looks up cached partition metadata, and forwards it to the partition leader, which holds its role through a lease. A write is acknowledged once a quorum of replicas has persisted the write-ahead log record. Each storage replica holds a WAL and a B-tree. When a node fails, DynamoDB adds a **log replica** holding only recent WAL entries. It joins in seconds and restores the write quorum. WALs are also archived to S3.
takeaway: To restore a quorum fast, replicate the log, not the whole database.
deeper:
**Why ack on the log:** Appending a record is sequential and cheap. Once a quorum has it, the write is durable, even if the B-tree catches up later. It is single-node write-ahead logging, lifted to a replicated group.

**Why log replicas exist:** With three replicas and a majority quorum, losing one leaves exactly two, with no margin. Rebuilding a full storage replica means copying a whole B-tree, which is slow. A log replica needs only recent WAL entries, so it joins in seconds while the full replacement rebuilds.

**Why the lease:** No other replica can become leader until the lease expires. So the leader can serve strongly consistent reads without asking the others each time.

**Why S3:** Archived WALs add a durability layer beyond the three AZ replicas. Every choice here serves the paper's theme: predictable performance, even during failures.

quiz.q: One of a DynamoDB partition's three replicas fails. Why is the partition at risk, and what does DynamoDB add first?
quiz.a: With two of three left, one more failure breaks the write quorum. DynamoDB adds a log replica holding only recent WAL entries, restoring the quorum in seconds.

mcq.q: When is a DynamoDB write acknowledged?
options: When a quorum has persisted the WAL record
When all three replicas update their B-trees
When the leader alone writes its B-tree page
When the WAL has been archived to S3
mcq.why: Quorum persistence of the log record makes the write durable. B-tree updates and S3 archiving follow later.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: A customer pays for 3,200 write units, uses less than that, and still gets throttled. How is that possible?

predict.q: Early DynamoDB: a table with 4 partitions and 3,200 write units. How much could one hot partition use?
options: 800 units
3,200 units
1,600 units

title: Throttled under the limit: DynamoDB's hot partitions
body: Early DynamoDB divided a table's provisioned throughput evenly across partitions. A table with 4 partitions and 3,200 write units gave each partition 800. Real traffic is never even. One **hot partition** hit its 800 and got throttled while the others sat idle. Worse, when a partition split for size, each child got half the throughput. Customers saw throttling even though their table as a whole was under its limit. The paper calls this its most useful lesson.
takeaway: Split a budget evenly across shards and skew will find the seams.
deeper:
**The flaw:** Capacity belonged to partitions, not to the table. Customers bought throughput for the table and expected to use all of it. A skewed workload, where a few keys get most traffic, concentrates on a few partitions, each capped at an even share.

**Growth made it worse:** As tables grew, DynamoDB split partitions to keep them manageable. Each split halved per-partition throughput. A growing table became more likely to throttle hot keys, with provisioning unchanged. From the customer's side, the database got worse as it grew.

**It generalizes:** Any system that divides a global budget evenly across shards fails skewed workloads, and skew is the norm: celebrity users, popular products, giant tenants.

**The fix came in stages:** Bursting, adaptive capacity, global admission control, then split for consumption. Each patched a weakness of the step before.

quiz.q: An early DynamoDB table has 8 partitions and 8,000 write units. One partition receives 60 percent of 5,000 writes per second. What happens?
quiz.a: That partition needs 3,000 units but owns 1,000 (8,000 ÷ 8), so it is throttled, even though the table uses only 5,000 of its 8,000 units.

mcq.q: Why did partition splits make early DynamoDB throttling worse?
options: Each child got half the parent's throughput
Splits paused all writes to the table
Splits moved hot keys onto one node
Each split doubled the table's cost
mcq.why: Throughput was per partition, so a split halved each child's share and hot keys hit the cap sooner.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: DynamoDB's second fix removed almost all throttling from skewed traffic. It still wasn't good enough. Why?

predict.q: How much throttling caused by skewed access did adaptive capacity eliminate?
options: Over 99.99 percent
About 50 percent
About 90 percent

title: Bursting, then adaptive capacity: two patches for skew

stat.label: skew throttling removed by adaptive capacity

body: DynamoDB attacked hot partitions in stages. First came **bursting**: a partition could spend unused capacity saved from recent idle periods. That covers short spikes only. Second came **adaptive capacity**: watch consumed versus provisioned capacity and raise the throughput of hot partitions in a throttled table. The paper says it eliminated over 99.99 percent of throttling due to skewed access. But it was reactive and best-effort.
takeaway: Patching a flawed abstraction helps. Replacing it is what finally works.
deeper:
**Bursting as saved credit:** Capacity accrues while a partition is quiet, and a brief surge spends it without throttling. A persistently hot partition has no quiet time, so it has nothing saved. Bursting does nothing for sustained skew.

**Adaptive capacity's reach:** It moved budget toward the partitions that needed it, and the 99.99 percent figure shows how well that covered the common case.

**Its two weaknesses:**
1. Reactive: it responded only after throttling began, so customers still saw errors while it adjusted.
2. Best-effort: it couldn't guarantee a hot partition enough capacity.

**Where it led:** DynamoDB stopped treating the partition as the unit of admission at all. Global admission control tracks consumption per table, so the per-partition budget question disappears.

quiz.q: Partition A idles for an hour, then gets a 30-second spike. Partition B is hot all day. Which one does bursting help, and why not the other?
quiz.a: Partition A. Bursting spends capacity saved during idle time; B never idles, so it has no saved capacity to spend.

mcq.q: What was the main weakness of adaptive capacity?
options: It reacted only after throttling had begun
It helped only very short traffic spikes
It split partitions by key range too slowly
It forced customers to pick new partition keys
mcq.why: Adaptive capacity was reactive and best-effort. Helping only short spikes was bursting's limit.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: DynamoDB finally let a table spend its whole budget on any partition. One machine could still melt. Why?
title: Global admission control, then split for consumption
body: Adaptive capacity patched partition budgets; **global admission control** (GAC) removed them. Request routers take tokens from a GAC service that tracks a table's total consumption, so a table can use its full capacity even if traffic lands on few partitions. But admission adds no hardware. So came **split for consumption**: when a partition stays hot, split it by key range, choosing the split point from the actual key distribution. Splits finish in minutes and spread the hot range across machines.
takeaway: Admission control decides who may spend. Splitting decides who does the work.
deeper:
**Capacity moves to the table:** The budget is enforced in one place, at the routers, before requests reach storage. Buy 3,200 write units and you can spend them on whatever keys you like.

**Why splitting is still needed:** If one partition gets most of the traffic, the machine hosting it can still be overwhelmed. Splitting divides the hot key range physically, so several machines share it.

**Why the split point matters:** It comes from the actual key distribution. A naive midpoint split could leave nearly all the hot keys on one side.

**Where splitting stops:**
1. One single hot item: an item cannot be divided.
2. Keys accessed in sequence: new traffic just moves to the newest range.

DynamoDB detects both patterns and does not split, avoiding pointless churn.

quiz.q: A table under GAC has plenty of unused capacity, yet one storage node is saturated by traffic to a range of hot keys. What does DynamoDB do, and how does it pick where to cut?
quiz.a: It splits the hot partition by key range, choosing the split point from the actual key distribution so the hot keys land on different machines. Splits finish in minutes.

mcq.q: What does global admission control change?
options: Capacity is tracked per table at the routers, not per partition
Each partition saves unused capacity for later spikes
Hot partitions are split at their key-range midpoint
Throttled partitions get their throughput raised reactively
mcq.why: GAC routers take tokens from a table-wide budget. Saving capacity is bursting; reactive raises are adaptive capacity.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: DynamoDB can split, rebalance and globally admit traffic. There's one hot spot it will never fix for you.

predict.q: One key gets more traffic than a whole machine can serve. What fixes it?
options: An application change or a cache
Splitting its partition further
Adding partitions to the table

title: No amount of partitioning fixes a single hot key
body: Sharding spreads keys across machines, but each key still lives on one partition. When one item gets more traffic than one machine can serve, splitting can't help: an item cannot be divided. Sequential access defeats splitting too, since new traffic keeps landing on the newest range. DynamoDB detects both patterns and declines to split. The lesson holds for every sharded database: fix a single **hot key**, like a celebrity profile, in the application or with a cache.
takeaway: The database can move a hot key. Only you can cool it down.
deeper:
**Why it belongs at design time:** A shard key can spread billions of keys evenly and still fail if one key gets a disproportionate share of traffic. The database can move partitions, admit requests globally and split ranges. It cannot make one machine serve more than one machine's worth of requests for one item.

**Fixes above the database:**
1. A cache in front absorbs reads of the hot item.
2. The application splits one logical item into several physical keys, for example spreading a counter across sub-keys and summing them on read.
3. For sequential-key hot spots, salt, hash-prefix or reverse the key.

**Ask it in every review:** What is the hottest single key, and what happens when it grows 100 times? A shard key chosen only for today's main query is the most expensive database decision to undo.

quiz.q: A live-event app keeps a global viewer counter in one DynamoDB item, and writes to it are throttled. Raising table capacity doesn't help. What do you do?
quiz.a: Split the counter into many sub-keys that each take a share of writes, and sum them on read. One item lives on one partition, so the database can't split it.

mcq.q: Which hot spot is beyond the reach of DynamoDB's split for consumption?
options: One single item receiving most traffic
A hot range spanning many different keys
A partition that has grown too large
Traffic skewed across a few partitions
mcq.why: An item lives on one partition and can't be divided, so splitting does nothing. Hot ranges of many keys can be split.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Amazon's 2021 Prime Day ran 66 hours and made trillions of DynamoDB calls. What did latency do at the peak?

predict.q: Prime Day 2021: DynamoDB peaked at 89.2 million requests per second. What was latency like?
options: Single-digit milliseconds
Hundreds of milliseconds
Several seconds

title: Prime Day 2021: 89.2M requests/s, single-digit ms

stat.label: DynamoDB requests per second at peak

body: Peak traffic is where tail latency tends to balloon. During the 66-hour Prime Day event in 2021, Amazon systems made trillions of DynamoDB calls. Traffic peaked at 89.2 million requests per second, and latency stayed in single-digit milliseconds. That is the paper's design goal, **predictable performance**, shown at extreme scale. The paper gives the numbers; it doesn't say which mechanism mattered most that day.
takeaway: Throughput is easy to brag about. Latency at the peak is the real score.
deeper:
**Why the latency matters most:** Plenty of systems reach high aggregate request rates if tail latency is allowed to explode. Holding single-digit milliseconds at 89.2 million requests per second is what predictable performance looks like in practice.

**The design behind it:** Leader-based partitions replicated with Multi-Paxos across three Availability Zones. Global admission control lets a table use its full capacity even when traffic lands on few partitions. Split for consumption spreads a persistently hot key range across machines. The published figures credit none of these individually.

**The philosophy:** The paper says to design for predictability over absolute efficiency, and not to let caches hide work the system must be able to do without them. A system that meets its targets only with warm caches can collapse when caches go cold during a surge, exactly when a peak event needs it.

quiz.q: Two databases both hit 90 million requests per second at peak. One holds single-digit millisecond latency; the other's p99 climbs to seconds. Which meets DynamoDB's design goal, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: The first. DynamoDB's goal is predictable performance. Throughput bought with ballooning tail latency fails users exactly during the peak event.

mcq.q: What was DynamoDB's peak request rate during Prime Day 2021?
options: 89.2 million requests per second
6.25 million requests per second
2.3 million queries per second
40 million reads per second
mcq.why: Amazon peaked at 89.2M DynamoDB requests per second. 6.25M is Venice, 2.3M is Slack on Vitess, 40M is Uber's CacheFront.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Your cache absorbs 95% of reads, and everything looks cheap and fast. Then the cache restarts.
title: Don't let a cache hide work the system must do
body: A cache can make a system look fast and cheap while hiding that the backend could never carry the real load alone. The DynamoDB paper puts it plainly: design for **predictability over absolute efficiency**, and don't let caches hide work the system must be able to do without them. So in every design review, ask one question. What happens when the cache is cold: after a restart, a failover, a sudden traffic shift?
takeaway: A cache you can't survive without is a single point of failure.
deeper:
**The hidden dependency:** Suppose the database normally serves 5 percent of requests because a cache absorbs the rest. The system is really sized for 5 percent. When the cache empties:
1. The full load hits the backend at once.
2. The backend overloads and requests time out.
3. The cache can't refill, because the backend is too busy to answer.

A brief cache problem becomes a long outage.

**What predictability costs:** More hardware, or slightly higher normal latency. What it buys: no cliffs. The system behaves similarly in good and bad conditions. DynamoDB's log replicas and global admission control fit the same philosophy: both reduce variance under failure and skew.

**Where to apply it:** Meta's TAO sits over MySQL. Uber's CacheFront sits over Docstore. A cache in front of user profiles is standard advice. Each time, confirm the backing store survives a cold cache.

quiz.q: A database handles 10,000 reads/s while a cache serves 190,000 more. A deploy flushes the cache, and the service stays down for an hour. Explain the spiral.
quiz.a: All 200,000 reads/s hit a database sized for 10,000. It overloads and times out, so the cache can't refill, and overload persists until load is shed.

mcq.q: Which design-review question follows from the DynamoDB paper's principle?
options: What happens when the cache is cold?
How much hardware can a cache save us?
Which eviction policy gives the best hit rate?
Can we cache every table to cut reads?
mcq.why: Predictability means the backend must handle the work without the cache, as after a restart or failover.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Aurora keeps six copies of every write, yet sustained 35 times more transactions than mirrored MySQL. How?

predict.q: Aurora keeps 6 copies of every write. In a test against mirrored MySQL, what throughput did it sustain?
options: 35× more transactions
About 3× fewer transactions
About the same

title: Aurora ships the log, never the pages
body: A MySQL instance on network storage writes many things per change: data pages, redo log, binlog, doublewrite buffer. Replicate that across zones and the network becomes the bottleneck. **Aurora** (2017 paper) asks which single thing fully describes a change: the **redo log record**. So its MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible engine sends only redo records to storage and never writes data pages over the network. A separate multi-tenant storage fleet applies them and builds pages itself, in the background and on demand.
takeaway: Ship the log, derive everything else. The log is the database.
deeper:
**Why the log is enough:** Redo records are the minimal description of a change. Data pages, doublewrite copies and the rest can all be derived from them. Sending only the log removes most of the bytes a traditional database pushes to remote storage, and that saving is multiplied by every replica.

**The bonus, recovery:** A traditional database replays its redo log at startup to bring pages up to date. Aurora's storage applies redo continuously, so crash recovery is almost instant.

**The numbers:** In a test, Aurora sustained 35 times more transactions than mirrored MySQL, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction, even though it amplifies writes six ways. Storage also streams continuous backup to S3.

**The one-liner:** A scale-up SQL engine on top of a scale-out log.

quiz.q: Aurora writes six copies of everything, yet does fewer I/Os per transaction than MySQL mirrored across servers. Resolve the paradox.
quiz.a: Aurora multiplies only small redo records. Mirrored MySQL ships full data pages, doublewrite copies, binlog and redo to each mirror, so its total bytes are far larger.

mcq.q: What does Aurora's database engine send to storage over the network?
options: Only redo log records
Full data pages plus redo log
Binlog events for each commit
Doublewrite buffer page copies
mcq.why: Storage builds pages from redo records itself, so pages, binlog and doublewrite copies never cross the network.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: A whole Availability Zone goes dark, yet Aurora keeps accepting writes. What arithmetic allows it?

predict.q: Aurora keeps 6 copies, 2 per AZ, and writes need 4. A whole AZ fails. Can it still write?
options: Yes, four copies remain
No, writes stop until repair
No, writes need all three AZs

title: 6 copies, 4 to write, 3 to read: Aurora survives an AZ
body: Aurora cuts the volume into 10 GB segments. Each segment gets 6 copies in a **protection group**: two in each of three Availability Zones. Writes need 4 of 6 acknowledgments. Reads during recovery need 3 of 6. Lose a whole AZ and two copies vanish, leaving four: writes continue. Lose an AZ plus one more node and three remain: Aurora can still read, then rebuild its write quorum.
takeaway: Pick quorums for the failures you expect, then repair faster than they recur.
deeper:
**Quorums that always overlap:** 4 plus 3 is 7, more than 6. Any read quorum includes at least one copy that saw the latest write.

**Why two per zone:** It targets a specific failure model. Whole-AZ outages happen, and so do independent node failures.
1. Lose an AZ: two copies gone, four left, writes continue.
2. Lose one more node: three left, enough to read and repair, not to write.
3. Rebuild a copy: back to four, writes resume.

**Why it holds in practice:** A 10 GB segment repairs in about 10 seconds on a 10 Gbps link. The window in which a second or third failure could hit the same protection group is tiny, so double failures during repair are very unlikely.

**The lesson:** Fast repair matters to durability as much as the copy count.

quiz.q: Aurora has lost AZ A entirely. Then one node in AZ B fails. Which operations still work, and what must happen before writes resume?
quiz.a: Three copies remain: enough for 3/6 reads, not 4/6 writes. A lost copy must be rebuilt to get back to four before writes resume.

mcq.q: Why does Aurora's 3-of-6 read quorum always include the latest write?
options: 4 + 3 exceeds 6, so read and write sets overlap
Reads always go to the writer instance first
Each AZ holds a complete copy of the latest data
The storage fleet serializes all reads by time
mcq.why: Any 3 copies must include at least one of the 4 that acknowledged the latest write.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Durability isn't only about how many copies you keep. Aurora bet on shrinking something else. What?

predict.q: How long does Aurora take to repair a lost 10 GB segment on a 10 Gbps link?
options: About 10 seconds
About 10 minutes
About 1 hour

title: Aurora's 10 GB segments heal in about 10 seconds

stat.label: to repair a 10 GB segment on 10 Gbps

body: Durability depends on how long you stay degraded after a failure, not just on copy count. Aurora splits storage into 10 GB segments, so each repairs in about 10 seconds on a 10 Gbps link. The window for a second failure in the same group is tiny, so double failures during repair are very unlikely. And because storage applies redo records continuously, **crash recovery** is almost instant.
takeaway: Repair time is part of durability. Small pieces heal fast.
deeper:
**A durability decision in disguise:** If repairing a lost copy took hours, another failure in the same protection group during that window would be a real risk. Ten seconds shrinks the window to almost nothing. Segment size looks like a storage detail but acts as a durability knob.

**Recovery without replay:** In a traditional database, a crash means replaying potentially large amounts of redo log before serving traffic. Aurora's storage is always applying redo in the background and can build pages on demand. The engine doesn't wait for a long replay.

**The performance paradox:** Aurora sustained 35 times more transactions than mirrored MySQL in a test, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os per transaction, despite amplifying writes six ways. It multiplies small redo records. Mirrored MySQL multiplies full pages, doublewrite copies, binlogs and redo logs. Six small writes beat many large ones.

quiz.q: A team proposes 1 TB segments for Aurora-style storage to cut metadata. Using the 10 GB in 10 seconds figure, what durability cost do you point out?
quiz.a: Repair takes about 100 times longer, roughly 17 minutes per segment. The window for a second failure in the same protection group widens, raising double-failure risk.

mcq.q: Why is Aurora's crash recovery almost instant?
options: Storage already applies redo records continuously
The writer replays its full log from S3 at startup
Every AZ keeps a hot standby writer running
Pages are written synchronously on every commit
mcq.why: Storage keeps pages current by applying redo in the background, so there is no long replay at restart.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Aurora scales storage across a fleet and reads across replicas. One thing still runs on a single machine.
title: Aurora's limit: one writer, so writes don't scale out
body: Aurora's classic design keeps a single writer instance per cluster. Every write goes through one machine running the SQL engine, so write throughput is capped at what one big machine can handle. Read replicas read pages from shared storage, and storage scales out across segments. Writes don't. It is **scale-up SQL with a scale-out log**: it scales storage and reads, not writes. In exchange, there are no distributed transactions and no global clock to manage.
takeaway: One writer keeps SQL simple. It also sets your write ceiling.
deeper:
**The price of simplicity:** With one writer there is no cross-shard coordination and no global clock. The engine behaves like ordinary MySQL or PostgreSQL, and applications keep full ACID semantics unchanged. The hard distributed problems stay confined to storage, which only replicates and applies a log.

**When it is the right trade:** Money and orders, when one writer is enough. In decision-tree form: multi-row ACID needed, and writes fit one big primary? Then Aurora, or single MySQL/Postgres plus replicas.

**When writes outgrow one machine:** Spanner-style NewSQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB) splits data into consensus-replicated ranges with distributed transactions. Vitess shards MySQL when per-shard ACID is enough. Both scale writes and pay with distributed coordination.

**The catch:** Aurora hides the storage problem so well that teams can forget the writer ceiling until peak traffic finds it. Know your write headroom.

quiz.q: An orders service needs multi-row ACID. Peak writes use 30 percent of the largest instance, and growth is slow. Aurora or Spanner-style NewSQL?
quiz.a: Aurora. Writes fit one big primary with headroom, so you get full ACID without distributed transactions. Revisit only if writes approach one machine's limit.

mcq.q: Which limit does Aurora's classic design hit first as load grows?
options: Write throughput beyond one big machine
Storage capacity beyond one disk
Read traffic beyond one instance
Replica count across three zones
mcq.why: One writer instance handles every write. Storage and reads scale out.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Meta swapped the engine under its main MySQL database. Apps kept speaking MySQL. How much did it shrink?

predict.q: Meta moved UDB from compressed InnoDB to MyRocks. How much smaller did instances get?
options: 62.3 percent
6 percent
About 20 percent

title: Meta's MyRocks: same MySQL, under half the servers
body: Meta keeps its core social data in MySQL. Its main database, **UDB**, holds tens of petabytes of likes, comments and shares. On flash, the bottleneck moved from IOPS to capacity, and InnoDB had three space problems: index fragmentation, weak compression, and 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead. Meta built **MyRocks**, a MySQL engine on RocksDB, so apps kept speaking MySQL. The migration finished in 2017.
takeaway: Change the engine, keep the interface, and no app has to move.
deeper:
**The results:** Instances 62.3 percent smaller than compressed InnoDB, 75 percent fewer bytes written, and fewer than half as many UDB servers. At tens of petabytes, halving the server count is an enormous saving.

**Why swapping the engine worked:** Applications, tooling and operational know-how built around MySQL stayed the same. Only the layer that lays bytes on disk changed. That works because the engine sits beneath SQL and replication, which mostly don't care how it works.

**How LSM answered the space problems:** Fragmentation from half-full B-tree pages disappears, because SSTables are packed full. Compression improves, because sorted, full files compress better than individually compressed pages with free space. The 13-byte per-row transaction overhead was InnoDB's third problem, the one MyRocks set out to escape.

**The bonus:** Fewer bytes written also stretches SSD life.

quiz.q: Your MySQL fleet moved to flash and runs out of disk long before IOPS, and apps can't be rewritten. What did Meta do in the same spot, and what did it gain?
quiz.a: Swapped InnoDB for MyRocks, a RocksDB-based MySQL engine, keeping the MySQL interface. Instances shrank 62.3 percent, bytes written fell 75 percent, and UDB needed under half the servers.

mcq.q: Which was one of InnoDB's three space problems for Meta's UDB?
options: 13 bytes of per-row transaction overhead
Tombstones waiting for compaction
Bloom filters using too much memory
Level 0 files overlapping in key range
mcq.why: Meta cited index fragmentation, weak compression and 13 bytes of per-row overhead. The distractors are LSM traits, not InnoDB's.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Caching Meta's social graph with plain memcache was hard to keep consistent. What must a graph cache know?
title: TAO: a cache that understands the social graph
body: Reading Meta's social graph straight from MySQL, or through memcache, was hard to keep consistent and efficient. **TAO** (2013) is a graph-aware cache and API over MySQL. It models data as objects (users, posts) and **associations**, typed edges such as "likes" or "friend". It is a two-level cache. Follower tiers serve clients. A leader tier per shard talks to the database and sends invalidations to followers. All writes to a shard go through its leader.
takeaway: A cache that knows the data's shape can keep it correct.
deeper:
**Why graph-aware:** A generic key-value cache stores opaque blobs. The application must track relationships and invalidation itself, and that is where inconsistency creeps in. TAO knows about objects and edges, so it can cache edge lists and update them correctly when an association is added or removed.

**Two tiers, two jobs:** Follower tiers replicate widely to absorb enormous read fan-out. The leader tier is each shard's single write path to MySQL, so it orders updates and tells followers what to invalidate. Consistency is eventual, with read-after-write within a tier.

**The scale:** A billion reads and millions of writes per second, reported in 2013. It is read-mostly by design, matching a graph viewed far more than it is changed.

**The catch:** MySQL stays the source of truth. The cache is fast, but the database must still hold every edge durably.

quiz.q: Two TAO follower tiers cache the same friend list. A user unfriends someone. How does the design stop both from serving the old list indefinitely?
quiz.a: The write goes through the shard's leader tier, which updates MySQL and sends invalidations to the follower tiers, so their cached lists get refreshed.

mcq.q: In TAO, what does the leader tier for a shard do?
options: Talks to MySQL and sends invalidations to followers
Serves most client reads from widely replicated copies
Runs Paxos to pick which follower accepts writes
Stores the graph durably in place of MySQL
mcq.why: Followers serve clients; each shard's leader tier is the path to the database and pushes invalidations.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Many Meta teams used RocksDB directly, each building its own replication and failover. What was wrong?
title: ZippyDB: replication built once, not by every team
body: RocksDB is a single-node library. So before **ZippyDB** (first deployed 2013), many Meta teams used it directly and each rebuilt replication and failover on their own. ZippyDB does that once: a general-purpose, strongly consistent key-value store. RocksDB is the engine. Data Shuttle, a Multi-Paxos library, replicates. ShardManager places shards. And each request picks its own consistency: eventual, read-your-writes, or strong.
takeaway: When every team rebuilds the same hard layer, build it once as a platform.
deeper:
**Layered sharding:** Physical shards are about 50 to 100 GB, each holding tens of thousands of micro-shards (**μshards**). The Akkio mapping moves μshards between regions to keep data near its users. Moving a small μshard is far cheaper than moving a whole physical shard, so data can follow users without big migrations. It is the many-small-logical-shards pattern in action.

**Consistency per request:** Strong reads go through the Paxos leader and may cross regions. Eventual reads can be served by any nearby replica. Read-your-writes sits between: a client sees its own updates without paying for global strong consistency on every read. The caller chooses, so no workload is forced into the most expensive guarantee.

**The platform lesson:** When many teams build replication on a raw engine, they repeat the same hard work and the same bugs. Netflix reached a similar conclusion about Cassandra.

quiz.q: A ZippyDB-backed profile page must show the user's own just-saved edit, but strong reads are too slow. Which consistency should the request ask for?
quiz.a: Read-your-writes. The user sees their own update without paying for strong consistency, which routes through the Paxos leader and may cross regions.

mcq.q: What does Meta's Akkio mapping do in ZippyDB?
options: Moves μshards between regions to keep data near users
Replicates each shard with Multi-Paxos
Chooses the consistency level for each request
Splits physical shards when they exceed 100 GB
mcq.why: Akkio relocates small μshards across regions. Data Shuttle handles Multi-Paxos replication.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Meta never replaced MySQL. It kept it and changed two things around it instead. Which two?
title: Meta's recipe: keep MySQL, swap the engine, add a cache
body: Replacing MySQL under tens of petabytes of social data would mean new query semantics, new tooling and years of migration risk. Meta didn't. Its pattern: keep the relational store, change the engine, put a smart cache in front. **MySQL plus MyRocks** provides durability and transactions. **TAO** handles graph reads at huge fan-out. **ZippyDB** covers simple key-value needs. Each piece fixes one weakness without forcing a rewrite.
takeaway: Improve what's under and in front of a database before replacing it.
deeper:
**The engine swap:** MyRocks kept the MySQL interface and operating practices while delivering big space and write savings.

**The cache:** TAO targets what MySQL handles worst, enormous read fan-out over graph relationships. Graph-aware invalidation turns those reads into cache hits, and MySQL stays the durable source of truth.

**The side store:** ZippyDB serves workloads that just need a replicated key-value store, which used to push teams into wiring RocksDB up themselves.

**The industry pattern:** Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of their storage engines:
1. Meta: TAO.
2. LinkedIn: Espresso routers.
3. Uber: the Docstore query engine.
4. Netflix: its key-value abstraction.

The engine is reused. The layer in front is where each company differentiates.

quiz.q: Your MySQL fleet struggles with disk cost and with graph-style reads at huge fan-out. Following Meta's recipe, what two changes come before any new database?
quiz.a: Swap the storage engine for an LSM like MyRocks to cut space and writes, and put a graph-aware cache like TAO in front to absorb fan-out reads.

mcq.q: In Meta's pattern, which component handles graph reads at huge fan-out?
options: TAO
MyRocks
ZippyDB
UDB
mcq.why: TAO is the graph-aware cache over MySQL. MyRocks is the engine, ZippyDB the key-value store, UDB the main database.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: LinkedIn's replacement for Oracle stored documents on plain MySQL. So where did the new ideas actually live?
title: Espresso: LinkedIn's Oracle replacement on plain InnoDB
body: LinkedIn replaced Oracle for many applications because of license cost, hardware cost and painful schema changes. The replacement, **Espresso** (introduced publicly in 2015), is a document store whose storage nodes run ordinary MySQL/InnoDB, keeping documents as Avro binaries with JSON schemas. The new ideas live around the engine. Stateless routers hash the partition key and forward requests. **Apache Helix** tracks which node is master for each partition and handles failover and rebalancing.
takeaway: The engine is a commodity. Routing and control are the product.
deeper:
**Change capture built in:** Databus, LinkedIn's change-capture system, streams changes for replication and for downstream consumers. Downstream systems follow the primary data without querying it.

**The data model:** Four levels: database, table, collection, document. Secondary indexes are local, one per partition.

**The local-index catch:** A local index is cheap and consistent to update, because it sits on the same partition as its rows. But a query by an indexed field that isn't scoped to one partition must ask every partition: scatter-gather.

**The 2015 scale:** About 30 applications, millions of records per second at peak, and hundreds of terabytes before replicas. Consistency is strong per partition, through its master, with master-slave replication via Helix and Databus.

**The pattern:** Espresso's engine is borrowed. Its routers, cluster manager and change stream are where LinkedIn's own work went.

quiz.q: An Espresso app looks up members by email, an indexed field, but the query isn't scoped to one partition. Why does it get slow at peak?
quiz.a: Espresso's secondary indexes are local per partition, so the lookup must scatter to every partition and wait for the slowest one.

mcq.q: What does Apache Helix do for Espresso?
options: Manages partition mastership, failover and rebalancing
Streams changes to replicas and downstream consumers
Hashes the partition key and forwards requests
Stores documents as Avro binaries on InnoDB
mcq.why: Helix manages cluster state. Databus streams changes, routers hash keys, and storage nodes hold Avro documents on InnoDB.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Some data can be thrown away and rebuilt from scratch at any time. Why store it in a transactional database?
title: Venice: a fast store for data you can always rebuild

stat.label: single-get queries per second at peak

body: ML features and "people you may know" results are **derived data**, computed by batch or stream jobs from sources stored elsewhere. LinkedIn's **Venice** (open-sourced 2022) is built for it. Writes arrive as full dataset pushes from Hadoop or nearline updates from Samza, through Kafka. Storage nodes run RocksDB. It optimizes for bulk loads and fast reads, not transactions.
takeaway: If you can rebuild it, you don't need to guard every write.
deeper:
**The scale:** By 2018 it had replaced about 500 Voldemort read-only use cases. The 2022 post reported 1,800+ datasets, 300+ applications, peak ingest of 50 GB per second, and 6.25 million single-get queries per second at peak.

**A write path shaped by the data:** A batch job that recomputes recommendations produces a whole new dataset. So Venice accepts full pushes and swaps them in: eventual consistency with bulk swap. Nearline updates from stream jobs cover changes between pushes. Kafka carries both, decoupling producers from storage nodes.

**Reads with no network:** The Da Vinci client keeps a local copy of a dataset inside the application process. That only makes sense because the data is derived and read-mostly: brief staleness is fine, and the copy can always be rebuilt.

**Why RocksDB:** An LSM engine suits bulk loading and compact storage.

quiz.q: Venice loses a node's copy of an ML-features dataset. Why is this a routine event, not a data-loss incident?
quiz.a: The data is derived. Its source of truth lives elsewhere, so the dataset can be recomputed and pushed again from Hadoop or Samza through Kafka.

mcq.q: What does Venice's Da Vinci client do?
options: Keeps a local copy of a dataset inside the application
Streams nearline updates from Samza into Kafka
Pushes full datasets out of Hadoop jobs
Manages partition mastership and failover
mcq.why: Da Vinci holds a dataset in the app's own process, so reads skip the network entirely.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: A team loads a fresh 50 GB ML dataset through its payments database every night. What's wrong with that?
title: Primary and derived data need different stores
body: Primary data is the source of truth: a user's profile, a payment. Lose a write and it's gone for good, so its store needs per-write durability, transactions and backups. **Derived data**, like ML features or recommendations computed from primary data, can be rebuilt from its inputs. Its store can trade per-write durability for bulk loads and read speed. LinkedIn's Venice shows a pattern many teams miss: these two kinds of data want different stores.
takeaway: Guard what you can't regenerate. Bulk-load what you can.
deeper:
**One store forces bad compromises:** Loading a freshly computed 50 GB dataset through a transactional per-write path wastes effort on guarantees the data doesn't need. It also competes with the latency-sensitive primary workload. The reverse is worse: primary data in a store tuned for bulk swaps risks losing records that can't be regenerated.

**Separate, each gets tuned:** The primary store invests in replication, write-ahead logging and backups. The derived store invests in bulk ingest, compact storage and fast reads. It recovers from failure by rerunning the job that produced it.

**The first review question:** What is the source of truth, and can this data be rebuilt? Answer it before choosing a database.

**In the decision tree:** ML features and precomputed results go to a derived-data store like Venice. Bulk-loaded derived data is one of the tree's main branches.

quiz.q: One transactional database holds customer orders and nightly-recomputed product recommendations. The nightly load slows checkout. What do you propose, and why is it safe?
quiz.a: Move recommendations to a derived-data store built for bulk loads, like Venice. They can be recomputed from their inputs, so they don't need the per-write durability orders do.

mcq.q: What property of derived data lets its store relax per-write durability?
options: It can be rebuilt by rerunning the jobs that made it
It is always smaller than the primary data
It is written by only a single application
It never needs to be read at low latency
mcq.why: Derived data's source of truth lives elsewhere, so lost writes are recoverable by recomputation.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Uber's Docstore runs MySQL in every partition, yet replicates with Raft. How do the two fit together?
title: Docstore: Uber replicates MySQL transactions with Raft
body: Uber's first scalable datastore, **Schemaless** (2016), was an append-only layer on sharded MySQL. In 2021 Uber described how it evolved into **Docstore**, a general-purpose distributed SQL-like database. A stateless query engine layer routes requests. A storage layer splits data into partitions of 3 to 5 nodes in independent zones, each running MySQL. The trick: Uber wraps MySQL transactions as the unit Raft replicates. The result is strict serializability within a partition.
takeaway: Don't rebuild a transactional engine. Replicate the one you trust.
deeper:
**Two proven parts:** MySQL supplies a mature local engine with transactions. Raft supplies consensus replication across zones. Each partition behaves like a single strictly serializable database copied to 3 to 5 nodes, so losing a zone doesn't lose committed data.

**Features on top:** Schemas, transactions, materialized views, and change data capture through **Flux**, which tails the MySQL binlog. Other systems can react to changes without polling.

**The 2021 scale:** Tens of millions of queries per second, 99.99 percent or better availability, tens of petabytes of operational data.

**The cache, built in:** In 2024 Uber added CacheFront, a Redis cache inside the Docstore query engine, kept fresh by Flux, serving over 40 million reads per second. Putting the cache in the query engine and refreshing it from the change stream spares applications from managing cache consistency themselves.

quiz.q: A zone holding one Docstore partition replica goes down mid-traffic. Why is committed data safe, and why do all replicas agree on order?
quiz.a: Uber replicates whole MySQL transactions through Raft across 3 to 5 nodes in independent zones. A committed transaction sits in the Raft log on a majority and applies in one order.

mcq.q: What does Flux do in Docstore?
options: Tails the MySQL binlog for change data capture
Replicates MySQL transactions with Raft
Routes queries in the stateless engine layer
Caches hot reads in Redis for the query engine
mcq.why: Flux is Docstore's change data capture, tailing the binlog; it also keeps CacheFront fresh.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Uber runs tens of thousands of Cassandra nodes. What hurt most at that size wasn't serving queries.
title: Uber's Cassandra: tens of thousands of nodes, three pains
body: Uber runs Cassandra for workloads that need high write throughput and TTLs. Its 2023 post described tens of thousands of nodes, hundreds of clusters of 6 to 450 nodes each, tens of millions of queries per second and petabytes of data. The main pain points were operational: unreliable node replacement, lightweight-transaction errors, and slow **anti-entropy repair**. Uber fixed repair by building a repair scheduler inside Cassandra.
takeaway: At tens of thousands of nodes, a rare chore becomes a daily one.
deeper:
**Why two stores:** Docstore gives transactions and strict serializability per partition on MySQL. Cassandra's leaderless LSM design gives very high write throughput and native TTLs, suited to time-ordered data that expires.

**Pain inherited from Dynamo:** In a leaderless system, replicas can diverge, so anti-entropy repair must reconcile them, the job Dynamo did with Merkle trees. At tens of thousands of nodes, slow or badly scheduled repair leaves data inconsistent for long stretches and burns resources. A scheduler inside Cassandra made repair routine instead of an external chore.

**Node replacement never stops:** With that many machines, some are always failing. Replacement has to be reliable and automated.

**Lightweight transactions:** Cassandra's compare-and-set feature adds coordination to a system otherwise designed to avoid it. Uber named its errors as one of three main pains, next to replacement and repair.

quiz.q: A leaderless store at Uber's scale runs anti-entropy repair slowly and irregularly. What user-visible risk grows, and why?
quiz.a: Inconsistent reads. Replicas accept writes independently and drift apart; until repair reconciles them, different replicas can return different values.

mcq.q: Which pain point did Uber fix by building a scheduler inside Cassandra?
options: Slow anti-entropy repair
Unreliable node replacement
Lightweight-transaction errors
Java garbage-collection pauses
mcq.why: Uber's 2023 post says it fixed slow repair with a repair scheduler inside Cassandra. GC pauses were Instagram's problem.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Take Amazon's leaderless ring and Google's storage engine and bolt them together. What are you good at?
title: Cassandra: Dynamo's ring on top of Bigtable's storage
body: Apache **Cassandra** came out of Facebook in 2008, originally for inbox search. It combines two designs. From Dynamo: the leaderless ring, with consistent hashing, tunable consistency and hinted handoff. From Bigtable: LSM storage, with commit log, memtable and SSTables. Any reachable replica accepts a write, and LSM writes are sequential, so it excels at high write rates across many datacenters. With no leader and key-shaped data, it is weak at transactions and ad-hoc queries.
takeaway: Inherit two designs, and you inherit both sets of limits.
deeper:
**What Dynamo gives:** Availability. No leader to fail over, writes accepted by whichever replicas are reachable, and per-request consistency levels that trade freshness for latency.

**What Bigtable gives:** Efficient storage. Memtable plus commit log for fast durable writes, immutable SSTables, and compaction strategies such as size-tiered and time-window.

**Where it hurts:** Without a leader, multi-row transactions are hard. Without a global index, queries must be designed around partition keys. Cassandra's classic secondary indexes are local, so a query on an indexed column asks every node.

**Who runs it:** Uber, Apple, Netflix and Instagram, with tunable, eventual consistency.

**Where it fits:** Write-heavy, time-ordered data such as messages and feeds, keyed by (user_id, time bucket). Bigtable and HBase sit on the same branch of the decision tree.

quiz.q: A team picks Cassandra, then needs "find all users in a city" across the whole dataset plus atomic multi-row updates. Why will they struggle?
quiz.a: Cassandra's classic secondary indexes are local, so a city query asks every node, and its leaderless design has no leader to coordinate multi-row transactions.

mcq.q: What does Cassandra take from Bigtable?
options: LSM storage with commit log, memtable and SSTables
Consistent hashing with tunable consistency
Hinted handoff when a replica is down
A single master that assigns tablets
mcq.why: Cassandra's storage is Bigtable-style LSM. The ring, tunable consistency and hinted handoff come from Dynamo.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Instagram runs one of the largest Cassandra deployments. Its pain was occasional very slow requests. Why?

predict.q: Instagram's Cassandra showed occasional very slow requests. What was the main cause?
options: Java garbage-collection pauses
Too few Cassandra nodes
Slow links between regions

title: Rocksandra: Instagram swapped out Cassandra's Java engine
body: Cassandra scales far: Apple said around 2015 that it ran over 75,000 nodes storing more than 10 PB. Instagram, a user since 2012 with one of the world's largest deployments, hit a different wall: tail latency. Cassandra's Java storage engine paused for **garbage collection**, reclaiming memory while slow requests stacked up. In 2018 Instagram built **Rocksandra**, swapping that engine for RocksDB and keeping Cassandra's distribution layer.
takeaway: Averages hide pauses. Your p99 never does.
deeper:
**Why Apple's number matters:** At 75,000 nodes, having no central leader or master on the data path is an advantage. No single component sits in every request's way. Apple is also a major contributor to the project.

**Why GC hurts storage:** Garbage-collected runtimes periodically pause to reclaim memory. A storage engine juggles many objects for memtables, caches and compaction. Those pauses surface as occasional very slow requests, raising p99 even when averages look fine.

**The fix:** RocksDB is written in C++ with explicit memory management, so moving storage into it removed that source of pauses. The distribution layer Instagram already knew stayed put.

**The recurring move:** Meta put RocksDB under MySQL. TiKV and YugabyteDB built on it. Instagram did the same inside Cassandra. The engine is a reusable part; the distribution layer carries the company-specific value.

quiz.q: Your Java-based storage service has fine averages but p99 spikes that line up with GC logs. Following Instagram, what do you change and what do you keep?
quiz.a: Replace the Java storage engine with a native one like RocksDB to remove GC pauses, and keep the existing distribution layer, as Rocksandra did for Cassandra.

mcq.q: Why did Instagram build Rocksandra?
options: To cut tail latency from Java garbage collection
To add multi-row transactions to Cassandra
To store more than 10 PB on fewer nodes
To replace Cassandra's leaderless ring
mcq.why: Rocksandra swapped Cassandra's Java storage engine for RocksDB to remove GC pauses. The ring stayed.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Netflix teams using Cassandra kept making the same mistakes. The fix wasn't more training. What was it?
title: Netflix hid Cassandra behind one key-value API
body: Netflix manages petabytes of data in Cassandra. Over time it saw each team using Cassandra directly repeat the same mistakes: data modeling, large partitions and retries. Its answer, described in 2024, was a **Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer** on its internal Data Gateway platform. Apps call a simple API, a map of id to a sorted map of items. The platform handles the backing store, mostly Cassandra, plus chunking of large values and **idempotency tokens** for safe retries.
takeaway: Encode a lesson in the platform once, instead of teaching every team.
deeper:
**Lessons, encoded once:** Large partitions, where too much data piles under one partition key, hurt Cassandra. Chunking large values and a constrained data model steer teams away from them. Retries after timeouts can apply a write twice. Idempotency tokens let the platform recognize a repeat and apply it once.

**A small API that covers a lot:** An id mapped to a sorted map of items fits many common patterns, such as a user's events sorted by time, while hiding Cassandra-specific details.

**Freedom to change underneath:** Because applications no longer talk to Cassandra directly, the platform can tune or change the backing store without app changes.

**The shared pattern:** It mirrors Meta's reason for ZippyDB. Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of their storage engines. The engines are shared or open source; the layer in front holds each company's operational knowledge.

quiz.q: A client times out writing to Netflix's KV layer and retries, but the first write actually succeeded. What prevents a duplicate?
quiz.a: An idempotency token on the request. The platform recognizes the retry as the same operation and applies it only once.

mcq.q: What API does Netflix's Key-Value abstraction expose to applications?
options: A map of id to a sorted map of items
SQL tables with global secondary indexes
Raw Cassandra queries with safety checks
A document store with JSON schemas
mcq.why: Apps see id mapped to a sorted map of items; the platform handles Cassandra, chunking and idempotency.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: YouTube's sharding logic lived inside application code and kept getting more painful. Where did it go?
title: Vitess: YouTube moved sharding out of the app
body: YouTube scaled MySQL from one primary, to read replicas, to sharding in application code, and that code kept getting painful. **Vitess**, begun at YouTube in 2010, moved sharding into a proxy layer. **VTGate** is a stateless proxy that speaks the MySQL protocol, parses queries and routes them to the right shard. **VTTablet**, a sidecar beside each MySQL instance, adds connection pooling, query safety limits and health checks.
takeaway: Sharding logic belongs in one proxy, not scattered through every app.
deeper:
**The rest of the system:** A topology service (etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul) records which shards exist and where. **Vindexes** define how a row's column maps to a shard: by hash, through a lookup table, and so on. Lookup vindexes are directory partitioning.

**Why the MySQL protocol matters:** Applications connect as if to one MySQL database. Routing that used to be scattered through app code now lives in one place, upgraded and operated independently.

**Why VTTablet matters:** Connection pooling protects MySQL from floods of client connections. Query limits stop a runaway query from hurting a shard.

**Online resharding:**
1. Copy data to new shards with filtered binlog replication.
2. Keep them in sync while traffic continues.
3. Switch traffic to the new shards.

Vitess graduated from the CNCF in November 2019.

quiz.q: A team needs to split one overloaded Vitess shard into two without downtime. What does Vitess do, step by step?
quiz.a: It copies the shard's data to new shards with filtered binlog replication, keeps them in sync, then switches traffic over to the new shards.

mcq.q: What is VTGate in Vitess?
options: A stateless proxy that speaks MySQL and routes queries
A sidecar that pools connections beside each MySQL
A topology store that records where shards live
A vindex that maps a column value to a shard
mcq.why: VTGate routes queries over the MySQL protocol. VTTablet is the sidecar; etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul hold topology.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Slack sharded MySQL by workspace, which seemed natural. What did its biggest customers and one feature break?

predict.q: Slack on Vitess peaked at 2.3 million queries per second. What was p99 latency?
options: 11 ms
110 ms
1.1 seconds

title: Slack on Vitess: 2.3M queries/s at 11 ms p99

stat.label: peak queries per second on Vitess

body: Slack originally sharded MySQL by workspace. Large customers created hot shards, and features like cross-workspace channels didn't fit a model where each workspace lived on one shard. Slack began moving to **Vitess** in 2017. By December 2020, 99 percent of its MySQL traffic ran there, peaking at 2.3 million queries per second (2 million reads, 300,000 writes), with 2 ms median and 11 ms p99 latency.
takeaway: The shard key that fits today's product can block tomorrow's feature.
deeper:
**Why workspace sharding appealed:** It is tenant grouping with a directory. Each workspace lives on one shard, found through a mapping, so most operations stay on one shard.

**How it broke:**
1. A very large workspace concentrated load on one shard: the hot-tenant problem.
2. Cross-workspace channels broke the assumption that related data lived together.

**What Vitess changed:** Sharding moved into a proxy layer, with vindexes defining how rows map to shards. Online resharding, filtered binlog replication followed by a traffic switch, can redistribute data while the system keeps running. VTGate speaks the MySQL protocol, so applications connect as if to one MySQL database.

**It took years anyway:** Begun in 2017, 99 percent of traffic by December 2020, with the last 1 percent still to go. Resharding a large live system is slow even with good tooling. A bad shard key is the most expensive decision to undo in a database.

quiz.q: You're designing a chat product and plan to shard by team. Using Slack's history, what two questions do you ask before committing?
quiz.a: How big can the largest team grow, since a giant tenant becomes a hot shard? And will any feature span teams, like cross-workspace channels, breaking one-team-per-shard?

mcq.q: By December 2020, how much of Slack's MySQL traffic ran on Vitess?
options: 99 percent
50 percent
100 percent
75 percent
mcq.why: Slack began moving in 2017 and reached 99 percent by December 2020, peaking at 2.3M queries per second.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB look like three different products. Underneath, they copy one Google paper.
title: CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB: three copies of Spanner
body: **NewSQL** means distributed databases that keep SQL and ACID transactions but scale horizontally. The three popular open ones follow Spanner's pattern. CockroachDB speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, with Raft per range, a leaseholder serving reads and writes, and the Pebble LSM engine. TiDB is MySQL compatible: stateless TiDB servers over TiKV regions, Raft with 3 replicas by default, on RocksDB. YugabyteDB offers YSQL (PostgreSQL compatible) and YCQL over Raft tablets on DocDB, built on RocksDB.
takeaway: Range, region, tablet: three names for one Spanner-shaped idea.
deeper:
**The shared blueprint:**
1. A sorted key space split into ranges of a few hundred MB.
2. Each range is a consensus group.
3. A transaction layer coordinates multi-range writes.
4. Ranges split and move automatically, so capacity grows without manual resharding.

**Raft instead of Paxos:** The unit is the same idea as Spanner's Paxos groups. All three also put an LSM engine at the bottom, RocksDB or the RocksDB-inspired Pebble. The engine inside the engine, again.

**TiDB's extra:** TiFlash, a columnar replica for analytics. Analytical queries run on a column-laid copy without disturbing the transactional row store.

**Where they fit:** Serializable or snapshot consistency with Raft per range. Pick them, alongside Spanner, when you need multi-row ACID and your writes don't fit one big primary.

**What actually differs:** Mostly the clock.

quiz.q: Your app is written for PostgreSQL, needs multi-row ACID, and has outgrown one primary for writes. Which open NewSQL systems fit, and what do they share?
quiz.a: CockroachDB (PostgreSQL wire protocol) or YugabyteDB (YSQL). Both split a sorted key space into Raft-replicated ranges with a distributed transaction layer, like Spanner.

mcq.q: Which local engine does CockroachDB use?
options: Pebble, a Go LSM engine
RocksDB, through TiKV
DocDB, built on RocksDB
InnoDB, under MySQL
mcq.why: CockroachDB replaced RocksDB with Pebble. TiDB uses TiKV on RocksDB; YugabyteDB uses DocDB on RocksDB.

section: 5.4 How big companies store structured data
hook: Spanner orders transactions with atomic clocks. Open-source databases don't have them. So what do they do?
title: NewSQL's real difference: where timestamps come from
body: Distributed transactions need timestamps that compare correctly across machines. Spanner uses TrueTime hardware; open NewSQL systems don't. TiDB uses a central **timestamp oracle** in its Placement Driver (PD): one service hands out every timestamp. Simple and correct, but it adds a round trip to one service. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use **hybrid logical clocks**, with no central service. The price: they must bound clock skew and sometimes retry reads that fall in the uncertainty window.
takeaway: No atomic clocks? Pay with a round trip or with retries.
deeper:
**The shared problem:** Make timestamps from different machines comparable, so transactions appear in one consistent order. Spanner keeps uncertainty to a few milliseconds with GPS and atomic clocks, then waits it out. None of the open systems assume that hardware.

**The oracle route:** If one service issues every timestamp in increasing order, ordering is trivially correct. The costs: a network round trip to that service, and a service that must be highly available.

**The hybrid-clock route:** Each machine combines its physical clock with a logical counter, staying close to real time while preserving causal order. Physical clocks can disagree, so the system assumes skew stays under a configured maximum. When a read meets a value whose timestamp is too close to call, it can't know the true order, so it retries at a later timestamp.

**The trade in one line:** A central service and certainty, or no central service and occasional retries.

quiz.q: Your cluster spans three distant regions. Why might hybrid logical clocks suit it better than one central timestamp oracle?
quiz.a: An oracle lives in one place, so transactions in far regions pay a long round trip to it. Hybrid clocks avoid a central service, at the cost of occasional retried reads.

mcq.q: How does TiDB assign transaction timestamps?
options: A central timestamp oracle in its Placement Driver
Hybrid logical clocks with bounded clock skew
TrueTime intervals from GPS and atomic clocks
Vector clocks merged by the application
mcq.why: TiDB's PD hands out timestamps centrally. Hybrid clocks are CockroachDB and YugabyteDB; TrueTime is Spanner; vector clocks are Dynamo.

hook: Hashing your keys spreads load perfectly across shards. Then someone queries last week's orders.
title: Hash partitioning: even load, but scans hit every shard
body: Every large system shards, and the simplest way is to hash. **Hash partitioning** assigns shard = hash(key) mod N, or places keys on a consistent-hash ring. Keys scatter evenly, so load balances and sequential keys never pile onto one shard. The cost: neighboring keys land on different shards, so a range scan across keys has to ask every shard. Dynamo, Cassandra, DynamoDB (on the partition key) and Espresso work this way.
takeaway: Hashing destroys order. That's both the feature and the bill.
deeper:
**Modulo versus ring:** With hash(key) mod N, changing N moves almost every key, forcing a huge reshuffle. A consistent-hash ring moves only the keys next to added or removed nodes. That is why Dynamo used a ring, with virtual nodes to smooth load.

**What it protects against:** Timestamps and auto-increment IDs, which would pile onto the last range under range partitioning, get scattered across all shards.

**What it can't fix:**
1. A single hot key still lands on one shard.
2. Any query that isn't a lookup by the full hash key, like "all orders between two dates", fans out to every shard.

**The common compromise:** Hash only a partition key, and keep rows within a partition sorted by a second key. DynamoDB and Cassandra use this shape, so scans inside one partition stay cheap.

quiz.q: An orders table is hash-partitioned by order ID across 64 shards. Product asks for all orders placed yesterday. What happens, and what would help?
quiz.a: The query asks all 64 shards, because hashing scatters one day's orders everywhere. A secondary index on date, or a partition key with time-sorted rows inside it, would help.

mcq.q: Why does a consistent-hash ring beat hash(key) mod N when you add nodes?
options: Only keys next to the new node move
Every key moves, but in parallel
Keys stay sorted, so scans stay cheap
The ring removes single hot keys
mcq.why: Changing N in mod N remaps almost every key; a ring moves only the neighbors' keys.

hook: A range-partitioned table keyed by auto-increment ID keeps splitting its hot shard. Why doesn't that help?

predict.q: A range-partitioned table keyed by auto-increment ID splits its hot last range. Where do new writes go?
options: Still to the newest range
Evenly across both halves
To the least loaded shard

title: Range partitioning: cheap scans, but a hot tail
body: **Range partitioning** gives each shard a contiguous key range. Adjacent keys live together, so range scans are cheap, and splits are natural: a range that grows too big is cut in two. The weakness is sequential keys. With timestamps or auto-increment IDs, every new write lands in the last range, creating a **hot tail**. Splitting only moves the tail. Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB, TiKV and HBase use range partitioning.
takeaway: Range sharding keeps order, so ordered writes queue at one door.
deeper:
**A natural fit for sorted engines:** B-trees and LSM-trees already keep data in key order. Bigtable's tablets, Spanner's tablets, CockroachDB's ranges and TiKV's regions are all contiguous ranges that split automatically as they grow. Resharding becomes a background process.

**Why splits don't cure the tail:** After a split, every new key is still larger than all existing ones, so writes go to the newest range. DynamoDB's split for consumption detects sequential access and declines to split for this reason.

**The fix is the key:** Salt it, hash-prefix it, or reverse it, so new writes spread across ranges. Bigtable's reversed URLs used reversal to group related rows; the same trick on sequential IDs spreads writes.

**The catch:** Scans in the original key order get harder, because consecutive IDs no longer sit together.

quiz.q: An events table is range-partitioned with a timestamp as the leading key. Name key changes that spread writes, and what they cost.
quiz.a: Salt or hash-prefix the key, or reverse it. Writes spread across ranges, but scans in time order now touch many shards instead of one.

mcq.q: Which systems use range partitioning?
options: Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB and HBase
Dynamo, Cassandra, DynamoDB and Espresso
Slack's workspace map and Meta's Akkio
Redis hash slots and ZippyDB μshards
mcq.why: Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB, TiKV and HBase split by key range. Dynamo and its kin hash; Slack's map and Akkio are directories.

hook: One customer grows 100 times bigger than the rest. How do you move just that customer and touch no one else?
title: Directory partitioning: a lookup table places every key
body: Hash and range schemes compute placement from the key, so moving one key means changing the rule for everyone. **Directory partitioning** stores placement instead: a mapping table says where each key or tenant lives. It is the most flexible pattern. Moving one big customer is just an update to its directory entry. The cost: an extra hop per request, and a directory that must be highly available and cached. Slack's original workspace mapping, Vitess lookup vindexes and Meta's Akkio use it.
takeaway: Compute placement and you get speed. Record it and you get freedom.
deeper:
**Built for uneven tenants:** Any key or tenant can go anywhere, so a few giants can get dedicated capacity in a multi-tenant system.

**Built for moving data:** Meta's Akkio moves μshards between regions to keep data near its users. Because placement is looked up rather than computed, a μshard can follow a user who moves.

**The operational weight:** The directory sits on every request's path. If it is slow or down, everything is. It must be replicated for availability and cached for speed, and caches must stay consistent with moves.

**Slack's lesson:** A directory at tenant level still inherits tenant problems. Mapping whole workspaces to shards meant large customers created hot shards, and data spanning workspaces, like cross-workspace channels, didn't fit. The directory made moves possible; it couldn't make one giant tenant small.

quiz.q: Your tenant-placement directory goes down while its caches are cold. What happens to the database, and what does that say about the directory?
quiz.a: Requests can't find their shards, so everything stalls even though the shards are healthy. The directory is on every request's path and must be highly available and cached.

mcq.q: What is the main cost of directory partitioning?
options: An extra lookup hop and a directory that must stay available
Range scans across keys must hit every shard
Sequential keys all land on the last range
Every key moves when a shard is added
mcq.why: Placement is looked up per request, so the directory adds a hop and becomes critical infrastructure.

hook: Updating a user's profile and settings together can mean a distributed transaction. One choice avoids it.
title: Keep one user's data together and skip 2PC
body: Cross-shard transactions need coordination like two-phase commit, which adds round trips and latency. **Entity grouping** avoids most of them: keep all the data of one user or one workspace on the same shard. Transactions that touch one entity then stay local. Spanner does this with **interleaved tables** and directories: related rows, such as a customer and their orders, share a key prefix and are stored and moved together. Grouping decides what lives together; the other patterns decide how keys spread.
takeaway: Put together what changes together, and most transactions stay local.
deeper:
