**Why it pays:** If a user's profile, settings and orders live together, updating several of them atomically is a local transaction on one shard. No cross-shard coordination.

**Spanner's mechanism:** A directory is a set of keys with a common prefix, and it is the unit Spanner moves between Paxos groups. A 50 MB directory moves in a few seconds. Interleaving child tables under a parent row keeps parent and children in one directory, so they always move together.

**The risk, uneven entities:** An entity that grows very large, like a giant tenant or a celebrity user, can outgrow one shard and become a hot spot. Slack's workspace sharding showed it: most workspaces fit, large customers created hot shards, and data spanning workspaces didn't fit.

**The design question:** How large can the biggest entity grow, and will any feature span entities?

quiz.q: An app groups each customer's orders with their profile in Spanner. A new feature transfers store credit between two customers. What changes about that transaction's cost?
quiz.a: It spans two entities, likely in different Paxos groups, so it needs two-phase commit across groups instead of a cheap local transaction.

mcq.q: How does Spanner keep a customer's row and their orders together?
options: Interleaved tables sharing a key prefix in one directory
A lookup table mapping each customer to a shard
Hashing the customer ID to pick a Paxos group
Copying orders into every replica of the customer
mcq.why: Interleaving puts child rows under the parent's key prefix, so they share a directory and move together.

hook: Going from 16 machines to 17 can force almost every row to move. One day-one decision prevents it.
title: Create thousands of logical shards on day one

stat.label: logical shards on 16 machines, day one

body: With hash(key) mod N, adding one machine reassigns almost every key: a massive, risky migration. The fix is chosen on day one. Create many small **logical shards**, for example 4,096 on 16 machines. Key-to-logical-shard never changes; only logical-shard-to-machine does. Growth then means moving whole logical shards, not re-hashing rows. ZippyDB's μshards and Redis's 16,384 hash slots follow this idea.
takeaway: Fix the key-to-shard map forever. Let only shard placement move.
deeper:
**Two mappings, split apart:** Key to logical shard is set by a hash function and never changes, so no row is ever reassigned by recomputation. Logical shard to machine is a small table that changes freely. Going from 16 to 32 machines just moves half the logical shards, each a bounded copy of one unit.

**Why resharding becomes routine:** Compare hash(key) mod N on physical machines: changing N from 16 to 17 reassigns almost every key. Small logical shards turn that migration into ordinary rebalancing.

**Pick the count once, pick it big:** The number of logical shards caps how many machines you can spread across without further splitting. Thousands leave room.

**Real systems:** ZippyDB layers it: physical shards of about 50 to 100 GB each hold tens of thousands of μshards, and Akkio moves μshards between regions. Redis Cluster's fixed 16,384 hash slots are the same pattern in open source.

quiz.q: You start with 4,096 logical shards on 16 machines and grow to 64 machines. How many logical shards per machine, and how many rows get re-hashed?
quiz.a: 64 per machine (4,096 ÷ 64). Zero rows are re-hashed: whole logical shards move between machines while every key keeps its logical shard.

mcq.q: Why do many small logical shards make resharding easier?
options: Keys never change logical shard; only placement moves
Each logical shard splits itself when it grows
Rows are re-hashed in small batches over time
Logical shards remove the need for routing tables
mcq.why: Growth moves whole logical shards between machines. The key-to-shard hash stays fixed, so no row is reassigned.

hook: You've copied every row to the new shards. Now you flip routing. What can still go wrong in that second?
title: Resharding: automatic splits, or copy, sync, cut over
body: Two more resharding approaches exist. **Automatic split and merge** of ranges (Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB, DynamoDB) is best for operators, but the system must be built for it from the start. **Online copy and cutover** (Vitess, most MySQL shops) copies data to new shards, keeps them in sync with replication or CDC, verifies, then flips routing. The flip needs a short write pause or careful double-writes.
takeaway: The copy is easy. The cutover second is where resharding bites.
deeper:
**Why automatic splits need a native design:** They work when the database owns routing and placement end to end. A range-partitioned system can cut a range in two, hand half to another server and update metadata without involving the application. Retrofitting that onto a system not built for it is very hard.

**Copy and cutover, step by step:**
1. Create the new shards.
2. Bulk-copy existing data.
3. Stream ongoing changes; Vitess uses filtered binlog replication.
4. Verify that old and new match.
5. Switch routing.

**The dangerous moment:** A write arriving during the flip could land on the old shard after copying finished, and be lost. So teams pause writes briefly, or write to both old and new locations during the transition.

**The effort is real:** Slack's move to Vitess took years even with good tooling. Plan for resharding from day one.

quiz.q: During cutover, a write lands on the old shard one second after the final sync, and routing now points to the new shard. What happened to the write, and how do teams prevent it?
quiz.a: It is stranded on the old shard and effectively lost. Teams pause writes briefly during the flip, or double-write to old and new shards through the transition.

mcq.q: Which resharding approach is best for operators but must be designed in from the start?
options: Automatic split and merge of ranges
Online copy and cutover with CDC
Double-writing to old and new shards
Re-hashing every row with mod N
mcq.why: Automatic splits need the database to own routing and placement end to end, as in Bigtable, Spanner, CockroachDB and DynamoDB.

hook: Your shard key serves today's main query perfectly. Why might it be your most expensive decision?
title: A shard key chosen for today's query can trap you
body: The **shard key** decides where every row lives. Pick it only for today's main query, and it may fail as the product grows. Before committing, ask three more questions. What is the hottest single key: a celebrity user, a giant tenant? What happens when it grows 100 times? Will most transactions stay in one shard? A key that looks fine now can create hot shards or force cross-shard transactions later. A bad shard key is the most expensive decision to undo in a database.
takeaway: Choose the shard key for the product you'll have, not the one you have.
deeper:
**Why it's so hard to undo:** Changing the shard key means moving essentially all data, rewriting routing, and often changing application logic that assumed the old grouping. An index or a schema field is cheap by comparison.

**Each question targets a known failure:**
1. Hottest key: no sharding scheme can split one key. DynamoDB's paper makes it the permanent limit.
2. 100× growth: skew compounds. A tenant using 1 percent of a shard today may overflow it later.
3. Transaction locality: cross-shard transactions are slow and complex. If common operations span shards, the key is wrong.

**Slack lived it:** Sharding by workspace served the early product. Then large customers created hot shards and cross-workspace channels didn't fit. The fix was a Vitess migration that began in 2017 and reached 99 percent of MySQL traffic by December 2020.

quiz.q: A marketplace shards orders by seller ID, which suits the seller dashboard. What three questions should the review raise before approving it?
quiz.a: Who is the biggest seller, and could it overflow a shard? What happens when it grows 100 times? Do common transactions, like one buyer's checkout across sellers, span shards?

mcq.q: Why is a bad shard key so expensive to undo?
options: Changing it moves nearly all data and rewrites routing
It forces every secondary index to be built twice
It forces the database to switch storage engines
It invalidates the write-ahead log on every shard
mcq.why: The shard key places every row, so changing it means migrating essentially all data and the app's assumptions.

hook: Keying events by timestamp feels natural. In a range-partitioned store, one shard ends up doing all the work.
title: Don't lead a range key with a timestamp
body: Range partitioning keeps adjacent keys together, and every new timestamp or auto-increment ID is larger than the last. Lead a key with one, and all new writes hit the newest range. That shard runs hot while the rest of the cluster idles, and automatic splits just move the hot tail. The fix is to break the link between arrival order and key order: **salt** the key, **hash-prefix** it, or reverse it, so new writes spread across many ranges.
takeaway: Lead with who, then when. Never lead with when.
deeper:
**The three fixes:**
1. Salting adds a small prefix, such as one of 16 bucket numbers, so consecutive writes land in 16 ranges.
2. Hash-prefixing puts a hash of a field like the user ID in front, spreading writes by user while keeping each user's rows sorted by time.
3. Reversing, as in Bigtable's reversed URLs, changes which part of the key varies first.

**The read-side cost:** "Everything in the last hour" now checks every salt bucket or hash prefix instead of scanning one range.

**Match the dominant access pattern:** Messages and feeds are keyed by (user_id, time bucket). Writes spread across users, while one user's recent messages stay a cheap single-range scan.

**Why splitting won't save you:** After each split, the newest keys still sort last, so the hot tail simply moves to the newest range.

quiz.q: A logging table uses a timestamp as its range key, and one shard is overloaded. You switch to (salt 0-15, timestamp). What improves, and which query gets more expensive?
quiz.a: Writes spread over 16 ranges instead of one. A time-range query like "last hour" must now scan all 16 salt buckets and merge the results.

mcq.q: How does keying messages by (user_id, time bucket) avoid a hot tail?
options: Leading with user_id spreads new writes across ranges
Time buckets expire before any range gets hot
The store hashes the time bucket before sorting
Each user's messages are copied to every shard
mcq.why: Writes spread by user, while time order within a user keeps recent messages together for cheap scans.

hook: Finding a user by email is trivial in one database. Shard it 200 ways, and the query must knock on every door.
title: Local indexes: cheap writes, ask-every-shard reads
body: A secondary index finds rows by a column other than the primary key, like a user by email. In a sharded database, a **local index** (document-partitioned) means each shard indexes only its own rows. Writes are cheap and consistent: row and index entry change together on one shard. But a query by email doesn't know which shard holds the user, so it must ask every shard and merge answers: **scatter-gather**. Tail latency grows with the number of shards.
takeaway: A local index is free to write and taxed on every global read.
deeper:
**Why it is the natural default:** No coordination. When a row changes, its index entry on the same shard changes in the same local transaction, so the index is never stale. Cassandra's classic secondary indexes and Espresso's per-partition indexes work this way.

**Where the bill lands:** Reads. Work grows linearly with shard count. Worse, the query waits for the slowest shard. As shard count grows, the chance that at least one shard is slow approaches certainty, so the typical query runs at the shards' tail latency.

**Where it shines:** Queries already scoped to one partition. Partition by user, index message time within each user's partition, and "messages of this user sorted by time" is served by one shard. No scatter-gather at all.

**The rule:** If the query names its partition, go local. If it doesn't, count the shards first.

quiz.q: A user-partitioned store has a local index on message time. Query A: this user's messages, newest first. Query B: all messages sent in the last minute, any user. Which is cheap, and why?
quiz.a: Query A. It names one partition, so one shard serves it. Query B doesn't, so it scatters to every shard and waits for the slowest.

mcq.q: Why are writes to a local secondary index always consistent?
options: The row and its index entry change together on one shard
The index is updated asynchronously after each write
A distributed transaction spans all index shards
Readers merge results from every shard at query time
mcq.why: Same shard, same local transaction: no cross-shard coordination, so the index never lags the row.

hook: A global index finds any user by email in one hop. So why doesn't every sharded database just use one?
title: Global indexes: one lookup, but writes cross shards
body: A **global index** (term-partitioned) is its own sharded table, keyed by the indexed value. To find a user by email, look up the email on the one index shard that owns it, then read the row. But writes pay. Updating a base row must also update an index row that usually lives on another shard. Either use a distributed transaction, as Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB do, or update the index asynchronously, as DynamoDB's global secondary indexes do, leaving it briefly stale.
takeaway: A global index moves the cost from every read to every write.
deeper:
**The synchronous path:** Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB update global indexes inside a distributed transaction. The index always matches the data. The price: every write touching an indexed column becomes a multi-shard transaction, with extra round trips and latency.

**The asynchronous path:** DynamoDB's global secondary indexes are updated asynchronously and are eventually consistent. Writes stay fast and single-partition, but a query through the index can briefly miss a recent change or return an old value.

**Pick the tolerable cost:** For a login lookup by email, a slightly slower signup write may be fine. For search, a briefly stale index may be acceptable. Either way, write the choice into the API contract so callers know whether an index read can be stale.

**The catch:** The index is sharded too. A very popular indexed value can still become a hot key on one index shard.

quiz.q: A user changes their email on a system with DynamoDB-style asynchronous global indexes, then immediately logs in with the new email. It fails once, then works. What happened?
quiz.a: The asynchronous global index hadn't caught up with the email change, so the lookup briefly found nothing. The index is eventually consistent.

mcq.q: How do Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB keep global indexes consistent?
options: They update the index in a distributed transaction
They rebuild the index nightly from base tables
They update the index asynchronously after commit
They store each index entry on the row's own shard
mcq.why: Synchronous distributed transactions keep the index exact, at the cost of slower multi-shard writes.

hook: Each of your 200 shards is slow only 1% of the time. How often is a query that asks all of them slow?

predict.q: A query fans out to 200 shards; each is slower than its p99 1% of the time. Odds at least one is slow?
options: About 87 percent
About 1 percent
About 20 percent

title: Fan out to 200 shards and p99 becomes typical

stat.label: of 200-shard queries hit a slow shard

body: A query that asks every shard is only as fast as the slowest one. With 200 shards and a local index, a find-by-email query fans out to all 200. If each shard is slower than its own **p99** 1 percent of the time, the chance at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99^200, about 87 percent. So the query's typical latency is roughly the shards' p99. A global index needs one lookup plus one read.
takeaway: Wait on enough servers, and their worst case becomes your normal.
deeper:
**Rare per shard, common per query:** Each shard is fine 99 percent of the time. But 0.99 multiplied by itself 200 times is about 0.13, so only about 13 percent of queries avoid every slow shard. At 500 shards, query latency approaches the worst shard's tail almost every time.

**It costs capacity too:** Each fanned-out query uses resources on every shard, even though only one shard holds the answer. High volume multiplies total load by the shard count.

**The global index flips it:** Two targeted requests, each subject only to its own shard's latency. The trade moves to the write side: a distributed transaction or an asynchronous update.

**The general law:** Any request that must wait for many servers inherits their tail latency. Keep fan-out off hot paths.

quiz.q: Your service fans out to 50 shards, each slower than its p99 1 percent of the time. Roughly what fraction of queries hit at least one slow shard?
quiz.a: About 40 percent: 1 − 0.99^50 ≈ 0.39. Fan-out turns a 1 percent per-shard event into a common per-query one.

mcq.q: With a local index over 200 shards, what sets a find-by-email query's typical latency?
options: Roughly the shards' p99 latency
The median latency of one shard
The index shard's lookup time
The average latency across shards
mcq.why: At 200 shards, about 87 percent of queries hit a shard slower than its p99, so p99 becomes typical.

hook: Login looks up users by email all day long. Which index you choose decides who pays for it.
title: Pick index type by query volume, and say if it's stale
body: For high-volume lookups by a non-key field, prefer a **global index** or a separate lookup table. Accept the cost: slower writes if updated synchronously, briefly stale reads if updated asynchronously. Then make that explicit in the API contract, so callers know what to expect. Keep local indexes for queries already scoped to one partition, such as "messages of this user sorted by time" in a store partitioned by user.
takeaway: Pay where the traffic isn't, and put the staleness in writing.
deeper:
**Where each index pays:** A local index pays on every cross-partition read. A global index pays on every write. For a lookup that runs constantly, like finding a user by email at login, paying on reads across hundreds of shards is ruinous. Paying once per write is affordable. For a query that names its partition, a local index costs nothing extra and stays perfectly consistent.

**The manual version:** A separate lookup table, say email to user ID, maintained by the application. Same single-lookup reads, same write-side choice between synchronous and asynchronous.

**The part teams skip:** Stating staleness. If an asynchronous index can lag, a user who just changed their email might not be found by the new one. Say so in the API, and callers can design around it, for example by reading the primary row after a write.

**In practice:** User profiles get a global email index plus a cache.

quiz.q: An API finds orders by tracking number, constantly, on a 300-shard store partitioned by customer. The team proposes a local index on tracking number. What do you recommend?
quiz.a: A global index or lookup table on tracking number; a local index would scatter every lookup to 300 shards. Document whether the index is synchronous or briefly stale.

mcq.q: When is a local secondary index the right choice?
options: When queries already name one partition
When lookups by a non-key field are very frequent
When the index must survive a shard failure
When callers can tolerate briefly stale reads
mcq.why: A partition-scoped query hits one shard, so a local index is cheap and consistent. Frequent global lookups favor a global index.

hook: Fourteen big systems, fourteen answers to one question: where do you put consistency, and what do you give up?
title: The big comparison: where each system puts consistency
body: Line up fourteen big systems and consistency spans a wide range. **Bigtable** is single-row atomic. **Spanner** gives external consistency via Paxos and TrueTime. Dynamo is eventual, with app-merged conflicts; DynamoDB offers strong or eventual reads per request. Aurora is ACID with one writer. TAO is eventual with read-after-write in a tier; ZippyDB is tunable per request. Espresso and Docstore are strong per partition. Venice is eventual with bulk swap. Cassandra is tunable. NewSQL is serializable or snapshot.
takeaway: Every system buys scale by spending some consistency somewhere.
deeper:
**Engines underneath:** LSM: Bigtable, Cassandra, and RocksDB in MyRocks, ZippyDB and Venice, with Pebble or RocksDB under CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB. B-tree: Spanner's B-tree-like files on Colossus, and DynamoDB. InnoDB: Espresso, Docstore, Vitess. Aurora uses a log-structured storage service; TAO sits on MySQL.

**Replication families:** Consensus per group (Spanner's Paxos; DynamoDB and ZippyDB's Multi-Paxos; Docstore and NewSQL's Raft). Leaderless quorums (Dynamo, Cassandra). Quorum storage (Aurora, 6 copies, 4/6 writes). File-system replication (Bigtable via GFS/Colossus). MySQL replication (MyRocks, Vitess). Master-slave with Helix and Databus (Espresso). Kafka pipelines (Venice).

**Strong only inside a partition:** Espresso, Docstore, Vitess and MySQL plus MyRocks all keep strong guarantees within one partition or shard. That dodges costly cross-partition coordination.

**Scale evidence:** 60+ products (Bigtable), 89.2M requests/s (DynamoDB), 35× mirrored MySQL (Aurora), 1B reads/s (TAO), 2.3M QPS (Slack on Vitess).

quiz.q: You need strong consistency but can accept it only within one partition, to avoid cross-partition coordination. Which systems from the comparison fit?
quiz.a: Espresso and Docstore (strong per partition), plus Vitess and MySQL with MyRocks (ACID per shard).

mcq.q: Which system offers external consistency?
options: Spanner
DynamoDB
TAO
Cassandra
mcq.why: Spanner's Paxos groups plus TrueTime commit wait give external consistency. DynamoDB is strong per partition; TAO and Cassandra are eventual or tunable.

hook: One app, a billion users: profiles, payments, messages, a social graph, ML features. How many databases?
title: One company, five kinds of data, several databases
body: Walk a 1-billion-user app through its data and one database stops making sense. User profiles, read-heavy and looked up by email: sharded MySQL (Vitess, Docstore or Espresso-like) or DynamoDB, with a **global email index** and a cache. Money and orders need cross-row transactions: Spanner-style NewSQL, or Aurora if one writer is enough. Messages and feeds, write-heavy, time-ordered, with TTLs: Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase keyed by (user_id, time bucket). The graph and ML features get their own stores too.
takeaway: Match each dataset's shape to a store. One size fits none.
deeper:
**The last two:** The social graph goes in a graph cache like TAO over a durable relational store, because graph reads have huge fan-out and far outnumber writes. ML features and precomputed results go in a derived-data store like Venice: rebuildable, bulk-loaded, fast to read.

**Why each pick:**
1. Profiles need point lookups by a non-key field, so a global index beats scatter-gather, plus a cache for volume. Ask what happens when it's cold.
2. Money needs multi-row ACID, so it goes where transactions are native.
3. Messages need write throughput and expiry, so LSM stores with time-oriented compaction, keyed to avoid a timestamp hot tail.
4. The graph gets Meta's pattern.
5. Derived data gets the primary-versus-derived split.

**The point:** No single database is best at all five, which is why large companies run several.

quiz.q: A new feature stores per-user "recently watched" lists: write-heavy, time-ordered, expiring after 90 days. Which store family fits, and how would you key it?
quiz.a: An LSM wide-column store like Cassandra, Bigtable or HBase, keyed by (user_id, time bucket), with TTL-friendly compaction such as time-window.

mcq.q: Money and orders need cross-row transactions. Which choice fits when one writer is enough?
options: Aurora
Cassandra
Venice
TAO
mcq.why: Aurora gives full ACID with a single writer. Spanner-style NewSQL is for when writes outgrow one machine.

hook: A new structured dataset lands on your desk. Which question do you ask first to choose its database?
title: The decision tree: ACID first, then access pattern
body: Start with the most constraining requirement: do you need **multi-row ACID transactions**? If yes, do writes fit one big primary? Then Aurora, or MySQL/Postgres with replicas. If not, Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB or YugabyteDB, or Vitess if per-shard ACID is enough. No multi-row ACID? Choose by access pattern. Key lookups with predictable latency: DynamoDB, ZippyDB, Espresso-like. Write-heavy, time-ordered scans: Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase. Bulk-loaded derived data: a Venice-style store.
takeaway: Ask the most expensive requirement first. It prunes the most options.
deeper:
**Why ACID comes first:** Multi-row transactions constrain the choice more than anything else.

**Scale up before scaling out:** One big primary avoids distributed transactions entirely. It is simpler and faster, so prefer it when writes fit. Pay for consensus-replicated ranges and distributed commit only when writes exceed one machine. Vitess is the middle ground when transactions can stay inside a shard.

**Without ACID, the pattern decides:**
1. Predictable point lookups: leader-based key-value or document stores with good partitioning and admission control.
2. Write-heavy, time-ordered scans: LSM-based wide-column stores.
3. Data computed elsewhere: a derived store built for bulk loads.

**A starting point, not an algorithm:** The tree encodes the core trades: consistency versus scale, lookups versus write-heavy scans, primary versus derived. Design-review questions refine it.

quiz.q: A ledger needs multi-row ACID, and its write volume is already three times what the largest single machine can handle. Where does the tree send you?
quiz.a: To Spanner-style NewSQL: Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB or YugabyteDB, or Vitess if transactions can stay within one shard. Aurora's single writer can't absorb the writes.

mcq.q: In the decision tree, which store fits bulk-loaded derived data?
options: A Venice-style derived store
Aurora with read replicas
Spanner with TrueTime
DynamoDB with a global index
mcq.why: Derived data needs bulk loads and fast reads, not transactions, so it goes to a Venice-style store.

hook: Five questions in a design review usually make the database choice for you. What are they?
title: Five design-review questions that pick the database
body: Product names distract; requirements decide. In a design review, ask five questions. What is the source of truth, and can this data be rebuilt? What is the shard key, and what is the hottest single key? Which reads must see the latest write? How do we add capacity without downtime? What is the **blast radius** when one shard, one zone or one region is lost? The answers usually pick the database for you.
takeaway: Answer five questions, and the database mostly chooses itself.
deeper:
**Rebuildable?** Separates primary from derived data. Venice shows rebuildable data can live in a bulk-loaded store without per-write durability.

**Shard key and hottest key:** DynamoDB's permanent limit and Slack's workspace sharding both live here.

**Which reads need the latest write:** Decides between strong consistency, per-request consistency as in ZippyDB and DynamoDB, synchronous versus asynchronous global indexes, and how fresh a cache must be.

**Capacity without downtime:** Points at resharding strategy: many small logical shards, automatic range splits, or online copy and cutover. Choose on day one, not as a retrofit.

**Blast radius:** Covers replication design. Aurora survives losing an AZ. DynamoDB replicates across three AZs. Spanner can span regions. A shard failure should hit only a fraction of users.

**The shift:** The questions move the debate from product names to requirements, where it belongs.

quiz.q: A team proposes one Cassandra cluster for both payment records and ML features. Which two of the five questions expose the flaw fastest?
quiz.a: Can this data be rebuilt? Features can, payments can't. Which reads must see the latest write? Payments need strong guarantees that Cassandra's tunable, eventual model doesn't give by default.

mcq.q: What does asking "can this data be rebuilt?" decide?
options: Whether it needs a primary store or a derived one
Which column should be the shard key
How many zones the replicas should span
Whether reads must see the latest write
mcq.why: Rebuildable data can use a bulk-loaded derived store; source-of-truth data needs durable writes and backups.

hook: Much of a database's hardware bill is set by code the app never sees. Three rules govern that layer.
title: Recap: engines, compaction and RocksDB
body: Three rules cover the single-node layer. First, the **storage engine** sets the per-node cost of reads, writes and space: B-trees favor reads and in-place updates; LSM-trees favor writes and space, and pay with compaction and read amplification. Second, compaction style is a workload decision: leveled saves space, tiered saves write bandwidth, FIFO fits TTL data. Third, reuse the engine: RocksDB runs under MyRocks, ZippyDB, Venice, TiKV and YugabyteDB. Companies differentiate in replication and sharding.
takeaway: Pick the engine by workload, tune compaction on purpose, build above it.
deeper:
**The frame, RUM:** Read, write and space amplification can't all be minimized, so B-trees and LSM-trees sit at different points of the trade-off. Meta's MyRocks migration shows the stakes: 62.3 percent smaller instances, 75 percent fewer bytes written, and fewer than half as many UDB servers once flash made capacity the bottleneck.

**Where LSM designs live or die:** Leveled compaction keeps space overhead near 11 percent with a 10× multiplier but rewrites data about once per level. Tiered rewrites less, keeps overlapping files and may need double space mid-merge. FIFO drops whole files for expiring data. Undersize disk bandwidth for compaction and you get Level 0 backlog, slower reads and write stalls.

**Why RocksDB is everywhere:** A correct, fast, crash-safe LSM engine takes years to build and needn't differ between companies. So the industry reuses it and invests in the distributed layers above.

quiz.q: A startup plans to write its own LSM engine to differentiate its new database. Given the industry pattern, what do you advise?
quiz.a: Reuse RocksDB or a similar engine. A crash-safe LSM engine takes years; companies differentiate in replication, sharding and query layers, not the single-node engine.

mcq.q: Which compaction style saves write bandwidth?
options: Tiered
Leveled
FIFO
Size-capped
mcq.why: Tiered rewrites each byte fewer times. Leveled saves space; FIFO suits TTL data.

hook: Bigtable, Spanner, Dynamo, DynamoDB, Aurora. Each bought scale by giving something up. What did each give?
title: Recap: distributed designs, sharding and indexes
body: Each big design traded something for scale. **Bigtable** split serving (tablet servers) from durability (GFS/Colossus). **Spanner** added Paxos groups and TrueTime for external consistency, paying with write latency. Dynamo (2007) was leaderless and eventually consistent; DynamoDB (2022 paper) uses Multi-Paxos leaders, B-trees and global admission control, and still can't split a single hot item. Aurora ships only redo records to 6-way, 3-AZ storage with 4/6 write quorums, scaling storage and reads, not writes.
takeaway: Plan for the hottest key and for resharding before you write row one.
deeper:
**The layer in front:** Meta, LinkedIn, Uber and Netflix all put a company-owned layer in front of their storage engines: TAO over MySQL, Espresso's routers, the Docstore query engine, Netflix's Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer. Those layers hold each company's operational knowledge: routing, caching, safe retries, data-modeling rules.

**The irreversible choices:** The shard key and the global-versus-local index choice are the hardest to undo, because changing either means moving or re-indexing all data.
1. Plan for the hottest key, since no partitioning scheme can split one key.
2. Plan for resharding from day one: many small logical shards, automatic range splits, or online copy and cutover.

**The through-line:** Every system chose where to put consistency, from single-row atomicity to external consistency, and gave something up to get scale: usually latency, write scalability or query flexibility.

quiz.q: Two years in, a team wants to switch from a local to a global secondary index and change its shard key. Why will this take far longer than their usual tuning changes?
quiz.a: Both touch every row: a new shard key means redistributing all data, and a global index means re-indexing into new shards, often breaking application assumptions too.

mcq.q: What did Spanner pay for external consistency?
options: Write latency from Paxos and commit wait
Transactions limited to a single row
Eventual consistency across regions
A single writer for the whole cluster
mcq.why: Every write needs a Paxos majority plus a few ms of commit wait. Single-row limits were Bigtable's; one writer is Aurora's.
